Fruit harvested winter from 5+ year trees. Premier rasayana and vitamin C source in Ayurveda; key ingredient in Triphala. Drought tolerant tree.
Bark and leaves used in Ayurveda for skin and digestive complaints. Sacred fig of Buddhism and Hinduism. Large tropical tree; not for small lots.
Aerial roots and bark used in Ayurveda as astringent and reproductive tonic. Massive tree; cultivate only on large plots in tropics.
Seed husks used worldwide as bulking laxative. Cool-season annual; sow as soon as soil can be worked. Harvest seed heads when fully dry.
Seeds harvested fall, dried for medicinal use as immunomodulator and digestive aid. Distinct medicinal use from culinary spice harvest.
Seeds harvested fall for use as galactagogue and blood sugar support. Easy cool-season annual; nitrogen fixer.
Unripe spikes harvested year 2+. Warming digestive in Ayurveda and TCM. Climbing vine; trellis required; greenhouse north of zone 10.
Berries harvested year 3+. Trikatu component in Ayurveda; potentiates other herbs. Climbing vine; tropical only.
Berries harvested year 4+. Anthelmintic in Ayurveda. Climbing shrub of tropical forest understory; greenhouse north of zone 10.
Selection bred for high withanolide root content; basis of KSM-66 extract. Treat as annual in cold zones; harvest roots before frost.
Nagori Rajasthan landrace prized in Ayurveda for fat finger-like roots. Sandy soil and dry growing season produce best roots.
Aerial-plus-root extract source; selection used for Sensoril branded extract. Distinct chemotype from root-only KSM-66 source plant.
Maharashtra landrace selection; vigorous foliage and large roots. Suitable for monsoon-mimic irrigation patterns.
Hypericin-selected European cultivar bred for elevated active constituents. Cut flowering tops in full bloom. Restricted in pasture areas.
Tall heavy-flowering selection prized for tincture production. Pinch first-year flowers to bulk plant before harvest in year 2.
Wild-type narrow-leaf selection bred for higher essential oil. Harvest leaves before flowering for tincture. Hot dry growing produces strongest oil.
Cultivate from seed or cutting to reduce wildcrafting pressure on overharvested wild stands. Drought tolerant; sandy lean soil, full sun.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds catalog descriptor; USDA NRCS

entries.notes: Aromatic California native sage used as smudge alternative to white sage. Bee plant; drought tolerant established. Avoid summer water.
California chaparral sage; silver leaves and lavender flowers. Cultivate as smudge alternative; full sun, no summer water once established.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering. Bitter cough syrup base; classic respiratory herb. Drought tolerant; can become weedy in pastures.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering. Antiemetic nervine in European herbalism. Strong smelling; self-sows readily.
Flowering tops used as gentle astringent and gynecological herb in European tradition. Spreads by stolons; partial shade, moist soil.
Whole flowering plant edible and gently astringent. Common cool-season garden weed; reliable early forage for pollinators.
Aerial parts used in European herbalism for sinus and ear conditions. Aggressive groundcover; can become lawn weed. Contain in pots.
High-carvacrol selections for oil of oregano. Harvest before flowering for highest essential oil. Lean dry soil intensifies oil.
High-thymol selection bred for steam distillation. Antimicrobial expectorant. Harvest stems just before flowering for highest oil yield.
Mat-forming creeping thyme. Aerial parts used in European herbalism for cough and digestion. Stone garden and path edges; full sun.
High-camphor selection for medicinal tincture and oil. Memory and circulation herb in Western tradition. Greenhouse north of zone 7.
Citronella-scented selection bred for high citral content. Strongest lemon scent in the genus. Self-sows; contain or deadhead.
German pharmacy strain bred for elevated medicinal constituents. Harvest before flowering. Self-sows readily; mulch to suppress volunteers.
Insect-repellent herb; never take internally as essential oil is hepatotoxic and abortifacient. Topical use only. Wet feet tolerated.
Classic high-menthol commercial selection with dark stems. Highest oil yield of common peppermints. Aggressive runner; contain in bed.
Pale-stemmed peppermint with finer flavor than Black Mitcham. Preferred for tea use. Contain runners with bottomless bucket.
Native Forecast or other carvone-rich selection for carminative tea. Gentler on children and elderly than peppermint. Contain runners.
Parent of peppermint; thrives in saturated soil and shallow water. Aerial parts used for digestive complaints in European herbalism.
Wild mint of Eurasia; gentler aroma. Aerial parts used as carminative tea. Contain spreading rhizomes.
Aerial parts harvested at peak bloom. Urinary tract herb in Western tradition; not the cause of hay fever (ragweed is). Spreads aggressively.
European pharmacopoeial species; preferred over American species for urinary tea. Less aggressive than S. canadensis. Full sun.
Anise-scented foliage; aerial parts make pleasant Liberty Tea. Eastern US native; sandy well-drained soil, full sun.
Flowers and ripe berries used for immune syrups. Distinct medicinal selection from culinary elderberry. Cook all fruit before consumption.
European elder selections (Sampo, Samdal) bred for higher anthocyanins. Used historically for flu prevention. Cook berries before consumption.
European hawthorn most used in Western herbalism. Berries, flowers, and leaves all support cardiovascular tone. Hedge plant; fruits at 5+ years.
European Pharmacopoeia hawthorn species; often two-seeded fruit. Used interchangeably with C. monogyna for heart tonics.
Eastern US native; small bright red fruits in heavy clusters. Substitute for European hawthorns in heart tonics where native plants preferred.
North American native with long sharp thorns. Heart and circulation tonic. Tough urban hedge; tolerates poor soil.
Midwestern US native with fuzzy leaves and large dark red fruit. Cold-hardy; substitute for European hawthorns in heart tonics.
Large hips harvested after first frost for highest vitamin C. Tincture and tea. Tough sand-loving shrub; salt tolerant for coastal sites.
Classic European hedgerow rose hip source. Harvest hips fully red after first frost. Pharmacopoeial source of rose hip powder.
Leaves harvested before flowering for astringent tea. Common gargle and diarrhea remedy in European herbalism. Pick from thornless cultivars.
Bark harvested from 2-year branches in spring. Source of salicin, precursor to aspirin. Wet feet tolerated; coppice for sustainable harvest.
Higher salicin content than S. alba; preferred for tincture. Coppice annually for bark harvest. Wet sites; useful for streambank stabilization.
Seed used after processing as vein tonic. Raw seed and leaf are toxic; only standardized extracts safe internally. Large tree; not for small lots.
Flower bracts harvested in early summer for nervine sedative tea. Large fragrant tree; flowers at 8+ years from planting.
Native North American substitute for European linden. Flower tea used as nervine. Large tree; bee favorite.
European Pharmacopoeia linden alongside T. cordata. Flowers harvested in early summer for nervine and diaphoretic tea.
Hybrid comfrey with reduced toxic alkaloids; valued as compost activator and fodder. Topical use only for skin and bone. Sterile; spread by root.
Parent of Russian comfrey; bristly leaves. Topical use only for sprains. Self-sows in disturbed ground.
Smaller European comfrey; tuberous roots used in folk medicine. Less aggressive than common comfrey. Topical use only.
Seeds pressed for borage oil (high GLA). Flowers and leaves used as adrenal tonic; topical only for leaf due to pyrrolizidines. Self-sows.
Aerial parts used historically as a diaphoretic; modern use limited due to pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Excellent bee plant; self-sows in poor soil.
Seeds pressed for omega-3-rich oil (Echium oil) used as flax alternative. Invasive in Australia; check local regulations before planting.
Leaves harvested in spring before heat. Mucilaginous respiratory herb in European tradition. Spotted-leaf shade plant; humus-rich soil.
Roots and aerial parts used historically as expectorant; modern use mostly topical and as natural detergent. Spreads by rhizome.
Greek mullein; flowering stalks reach 8 ft. Flowers infused in oil for ear complaints. Leaves used as lung-soothing tea. Biennial.
European pharmacopoeial mullein with bright orange flowers. Used like V. thapsus for cough and ear oil. Self-sows.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering. Bitter nervine in European herbalism. Distinct from blue vervain (V. hastata). Self-sows.
North American native nervine with intensely bitter taste. Used for tension and tight muscles. Wet meadow species; tolerates clay.
Aerial parts harvested when seed pods inflate. Powerful respiratory antispasmodic; emetic in higher doses. Use only with qualified guidance.
Rhizomes harvested year 7+. At-risk wild; cultivate only and avoid wildcrafting. Astringent gynecological herb. Deep shade, humus.
Rhizome harvested year 5+. Strong uterine herb; use only with qualified guidance. United Plant Savers at-risk; cultivate from seed.
Rhizome harvested year 4 to 6 from cultivated stock only. Wild populations critically threatened (CITES II). Deep shade, deep humus.
entries.source: United Plant Savers cultivation guide; USDA NRCS

entries.notes: Rhizome harvested year 3 to 4. United Plant Savers at-risk; cultivate only. Topical use only; internal use restricted and unsafe.
Rhizome harvested year 3+. Carminative used by indigenous peoples of eastern North America. Deep shade groundcover; humus-rich soil.
Glossy evergreen leaves; rhizome used historically as emetic. Use only with qualified guidance; modern use limited. Deep shade.
Rhizome harvested fall year 2 for astringent gargle and diarrhea remedy. Cool moist meadow plant; tolerates wet feet.
Roots harvested fall year 1 or 2 as iron-rich alterative and gentle laxative. Common pasture weed; deep taproot tolerates poor soil.
Leaves rubbed on nettle stings; roots used similarly to yellow dock. Considered noxious weed in some jurisdictions; check before planting.
Whole plant used in Western herbalism. Roots dug in fall for liver tonic; leaves spring for diuretic. Improved seed selections yield bigger roots.
Roots harvested fall year 1 for bitter liver tonic and inulin source. Distinct medicinal use from coffee substitute or witloof culinary.
First-year roots harvested fall for blood-purifying alterative. Loose deep soil produces longest cleanest roots.
Smaller wild burdock; first-year roots used similarly to A. lappa. Burs can mat in livestock fleece; manage seed heads.
High alpine species used in TCM as hong jing tian. Stronger salidroside content than R. rosea. Cold winters and cool summers required.
Far East Asian rhodiola; vigorous performer in cold continental climates. Roots harvested year 4+ for adaptogen extract.
Higher-eleutheroside selection bred for tincture production. Bark and roots harvested year 4+. Spiny shrub; partial shade preferred.
Roots harvested year 5 to 7. Warming qi tonic in TCM; distinct from American ginseng. Deep shade, deep humus, slow cool growth.
Wild populations threatened; cultivate from seed only. Roots harvested year 5 to 8 under 70% shade. Cooler yin tonic than Asian ginseng.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; United Plant Savers

entries.notes: Bamboo ginseng; thinner rhizomes than other Panax species. Lung-supporting tonic in Japanese kampo medicine. Cool shaded mountain forest.
Rare highland Vietnamese ginseng with majonoside-R2; harvested year 6+. CITES-regulated; cultivate from licensed seed only.
Self-fertile schisandra selection; fruits in year 2 to 3 without partner plant. Climbing vine; trellis required. Five-flavor adaptogen tonic.
Russian commercial selection bred for heavy fruit set and high lignan content. Pair with male plant for best yield.
Standard pharmacopoeial astragalus; roots harvested year 3 or 4. Premier qi tonic in TCM. Deep loose soil, full sun, low water.
Synonym A. membranaceus var. mongholicus; many references treat as primary medicinal type. Cold steppe origin; sandy soil, full sun.
Synonym of A. membranaceus per some treatments; chemotype with elevated astragaloside. Roots harvested year 3+.
Female cordifolia-type vine bred for higher saponin content. Aerial parts harvested for tea (immortality herb). Trellis or trailing.
Male pollinator vine for fruit and seed production from female plants. Foliage equally usable for tea. Vigorous climber; trellis required.
Indian large-leaf variant traditionally used for memory and skin in Ayurveda. Distinct cultivation pattern from base gotu kola for higher asiaticosides.

windows.notes: Indoor liquid or grain culture

entries.notes: Wild caterpillar fungus is unsustainable; cultivated mycelium-on-grain product is the accessible alternative. Climate-controlled fruiting chamber.

windows.notes: Inoculate living birch with sclerotium plug

entries.notes: Sustainable alternative to wildcrafting; inoculate live birch with plug spawn for harvest in 5 to 10 years. Cold-climate species only.

windows.notes: Inoculate standing or recently fallen conifer logs

entries.notes: Conk fungus of old-growth conifers; cultivation pioneered to relieve wild pressure. Slow grower; sustainable harvest after 5+ years.

windows.notes: Inoculate hardwood logs late spring

entries.notes: High-PSK and PSP chemotype selected for immune extract production. Fruits in 6 to 12 months on hardwood logs.

windows.notes: Inoculate oak logs late spring

entries.notes: Classic red reishi strain for ling zhi tea and tincture. Buried log technique increases yield. Fruit on oak in 6 to 8 months from inoculation.
Black-bodied reishi species, considered higher quality than G. lucidum in some TCM traditions. Cultivated similarly on hardwood.
Massive tropical Ganoderma species; bright yellow fruiting bodies. Less common in commerce; cultivate on tropical hardwood.
entries.source: Field & Forest Products tropical cultivation guide

windows.notes: Year-round indoor block cultivation

entries.notes: Strain selected for ergothioneine and beta-glucan content. Indoor block grown under climate control. Medicinal use distinct from culinary harvest.

windows.notes: Year-round indoor block cultivation

entries.notes: Selected for elevated erinacines and hericenones (NGF stimulators). Indoor block or log cultivation; harvest before spines elongate fully.
High-lentinan strain selected for immune extract use. Log-grown for highest medicinal compound concentration. Distinct from culinary strains.
Most common maca color; balanced adaptogenic root. Cool growing season required (high altitude or alpine zones). Sow direct in cool soil.
Rarer maca phenotype; traditionally favored for hormonal balance. Cool growing season required. Distinguishable by red-purple hypocotyl.
Least common maca color; valued for stamina and cognition support. Cool growing season required. Yields slightly lower than yellow maca.
Roots harvested year 2 or 3. Brazilian rainforest adaptogen with ecdysteroids. Climbing perennial; needs trellis and tropical heat.
Aerial parts used in Southern African medicine. Drought tolerant legume; full sun, sandy soil. Bright orange-red flowers with inflated pods.
Standard yellow culinary ginger grown specifically for medicinal use; harvest mature rhizome after foliage dies back. High-gingerol selections preferred.
Pale fleshed ginger variant; milder flavor and lower gingerol but used in traditional medicine for nausea and warmth. Mulch heavily.
Edible flower buds harvested late summer; aromatic digestive in Japanese tradition. Cold-hardier than common ginger; shade tolerant.
Large rhizome used in Thai cooking and Indian medicine. Distinct from culinary galangal entry; warming digestive aid. Rich moist soil, partial shade.
Smaller red-skinned rhizome; primary galangal in TCM (gao liang jiang). Warming digestive. Less common in commerce than greater galangal.
Smaller Curcuma species; rhizomes used in Thai folk medicine for digestion. Ornamental pink-bracted flowers. Rich moist soil, partial shade.
South Indian commercial cultivar; large rhizome with moderate curcumin. Standard for culinary trade; also used medicinally in Ayurveda.
Indian high-curcumin cultivar (around 4 to 5%) bred for medicinal extract industry. Yields well in tropical lowland.
entries.source: Indian Institute of Spices Research bulletin

entries.notes: Indian short-duration turmeric cultivar; suitable for shorter tropical growing seasons. Curcumin around 3 to 4%.
entries.source: Indian Institute of Spices Research bulletin

entries.notes: True source of citronella oil; distinct from lemongrass. Leaves harvested for steam distillation. Greenhouse north of zone 9.
Cochin grass; main source of medicinal lemongrass oil with high citral. Distinct from West Indian C. citratus. Sandy loam, full sun.
Leaves used in Ayurveda for digestion and diabetes support. Small tree; greenhouse north of zone 9. Selections for high carbazole alkaloid content.
Seeds and whole plant used in TCM as jiu zi for kidney yang. Cold hardy perennial onion family; harvest seeds when capsules ripen black.
European woodland garlic; leaves harvested spring before flowering for cardiovascular tonic salad. Shade-loving; naturalizes by seed and bulb.
Mountain ramps relative used historically as scurvy remedy. Slower to multiply than ramsons; bulbs harvested year 2+. Cool moist shade.
Egyptian perennial leek; leaves cut throughout growing season. Traditional medicinal food for digestion and cardiovascular tone. Hardy.
Seeds harvested for carminative tea and bitter formulas. High-anethole selections preferred for medicinal use. Distinct from culinary fennel seed.
Annual; seeds harvested fall for carminative tea and cough syrup. Distinct from star anise. Direct sow; doesn't transplant well.
Fruit harvested from 7+ year trees. Source of shikimic acid (oseltamivir precursor). Avoid I. anisatum which is toxic.
Flower buds harvested from 7+ year trees. Source of eugenol; topical anesthetic and digestive carminative. Tropical only.
Inner bark of 3+ year coppice stems harvested as quills. Lower coumarin than cassia; preferred for daily medicinal use.
Bark and twigs (gui zhi) used as warming herbs in TCM. Higher coumarin than Ceylon cinnamon; use medicinally not daily culinary.
Vietnamese cassia with highest cinnamaldehyde content; strongest flavor. Bark harvested from 5+ year trees by coppice.
Seed kernel and red aril (mace) harvested from 7+ year trees. Warming digestive in small doses; toxic in large doses. Dioecious; need male.
Pods harvested year 3+. Carminative digestive in Ayurveda. Understory tropical herb; deep shade, high humidity, rich moist soil.
Larger pods smoke-dried; used in TCM (cao guo) and Indian cooking. Hardier than green cardamom; subtropical Himalayan understory.

windows.notes: Plant corms in late summer for fall flowering

entries.notes: Italian saffron landrace prized for long deep red stigmas. Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained soil; lift every 3 to 4 years.

windows.notes: Plant corms late summer

entries.notes: Kashmiri saffron grade with highest crocin and safranal content. Requires cold winter and hot dry summer. Karewa soil mimic for best yield.
Cultivated only species (no wild form); shorter pods with cherry-like notes from heliotropin. Climbing orchid; tropical only or heated greenhouse.
Pharmacopoeial dong quai strain; harvest roots fall year 2 before flowering. Use fresh seed; viability drops fast. Cool humid mountain conditions.

windows.notes: Fall sow with fresh seed

entries.notes: Roots harvested fall year 1 or spring year 2 as carminative aromatic bitter. Stems candied. Distinct European species from Chinese dong quai.
Deep wine-red yarrow with classic medicinal essential oil. Cut flowering tops for tincture. Spreads by rhizome; full sun, dry soil.
Cherry-red yarrow strain; medicinal use parallel to white yarrow. Fades to pink in summer heat. Cut spent stems to encourage rebloom.
Large pure white yarrow with strong medicinal aroma. Excellent for tincture and infusion. Drought tolerant; cut after first flower flush.
European wetland yarrow relative; powdered root historically used as sternutatory. Tolerates wet feet; spreads by stolons.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering as astringent and liver-supporting herb. Bach flower; tall yellow spikes in meadow gardens.
Aerial parts harvested in flower for gynecological astringent tea. Pleated leaves hold dewdrops; charming garden plant.
Roots harvested fall year 2 for demulcent cold infusion. Tall pink-flowered perennial; tolerates wet feet and saline soils.
Leaves and flowers used as gentle demulcent and laxative. Pink-purple striped flowers; self-sows readily; salad herb also.
Pink-flowered perennial mallow with mucilaginous leaves; gentle demulcent like marshmallow. Self-sows in disturbed ground.
Roots harvested fall for stimulant decongestant. Sinus-clearing wasabi-like effect from glucosinolates. Aggressive spreader; isolate in bed.
Flowers harvested year 2+ for topical bruise oil. Acid sandy soil at higher elevation; wild populations threatened. Topical use only.
American arnica relative with similar sesquiterpene lactones; easier in cultivation than A. montana. Topical use only; tolerates richer soil.
Aerial parts harvested before flowering for dream herb and bitter digestive. Aggressive rhizome spread; contain in bed.
Bitter tonic and vermifuge in European tradition; ingredient in absinthe. Aerial parts harvested at flowering. Use briefly, with guidance.
Smaller silvery wormwood with milder bitterness; classic vermouth and absinthe ingredient. Aerial parts harvested before flowering.
Aromatic gray-green foliage; bitter aerial parts used as moth repellent and digestive bitter. Shrubby subshrub; cut hard in spring.
Wild tarragon; seed-grown form used historically for digestive aid and blood sugar support. Coarser flavor than culinary French tarragon clone.
Roots harvested year 2 or 3 as expectorant and diaphoretic in Western tradition. Native milkweed; monarch host. Deep taproot, no division.
Root bark and berries used for berberine alkaloid. Banned in some grain-growing regions as wheat rust host; check before planting.
Roots and root bark used for berberine; alternative to overharvested goldenseal. Pacific Northwest native; partial shade evergreen shrub.
Low-growing Oregon grape relative; root bark contains berberine. Cool moist forest understory; shade groundcover.
German pharmacopoeial calendula with deep orange double flowers and high resin. Picked at peak bloom and dried in shade.
Whole plant harvested at fruiting (purse-shaped seedpods) as hemostatic herb in Western tradition. Common garden weed; self-sows.
Flowers used historically as eye wash and mild astringent. Self-sows readily in poor soil. Bee plant; classic European cornfield flower.
Double-flowered Roman chamomile; mat-forming perennial. Flowers used for infused oil for topical use; less bitter than German chamomile.
Yellow latex used topically on warts. Internal use restricted in many countries due to hepatotoxicity. Self-sows; partial shade.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering as bitter digestive and galactagogue. Annual; self-sows. Distinct from milk thistle.
Aerial parts contain cardiac glycosides; use only with qualified guidance. Highly toxic. Spreads aggressively by pip rhizomes; shade.
Historically used for asthma; highly toxic anticholinergic. Restricted or banned in many jurisdictions; verify legality before planting.
Leaves contain cardiac glycosides used as digoxin source; deadly without precise dosing. Cultivation for pharmaceutical use only; not home apothecary.
Main commercial source of digoxin and lanatosides. Higher alkaloid content than D. purpurea. Pharmaceutical cultivation only.
Aerial parts contain salicylates; classic anti-inflammatory tea. Wet meadow species; tolerates clay. Fragrant cream flowers in midsummer.
Aerial parts used as bile-flow stimulant and skin alterative. Annual; cool season; self-sows in disturbed garden soil.
Aerial parts harvested fresh in spring as lymphatic mover. Sticky climbing annual; self-sows. Use fresh or freeze; dried form less active.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering; coumarin scent develops on drying. Used in May wine; limit internal use due to coumarin. Shade groundcover.
Rhizomes harvested fall for astringent gargle and hemostatic. North American native; woodland understory; partial shade.
Clove-scented root harvested in spring or fall as astringent. Self-sows; partial shade tolerant.
Strobiles harvested late summer for sedative tincture and sleep pillows. Long-day photoperiod requires 6+ hours sun. Sturdy 18 ft trellis.
Whole plant harvested for skin and nerve tonic; smaller-leaf Southeast Asian variant. Wet feet tolerated; spreads by stolons; partial shade.
Flowering tops harvested for expectorant tea and tincture. Bitter aromatic Lamiaceae; full sun, lean alkaline soil intensifies oil.
Roots harvested fall year 2 for lung-warming expectorant. Tall yellow-flowered perennial. Deep loose soil for long roots.
Rhizomes harvested year 2+ for lymphatic and liver work; emetic in larger doses. North American native; wet site or pond margin.
Pharmacopoeial lavender vera bred for high linalool. Flowers harvested at peak bloom for essential oil and tincture. Lean alkaline soil.
Hybrid lavender with higher essential oil yield but more camphor than true lavender. Used for cleaning products and salve infusions.
Leaves harvested for traditional indigenous tea; contains ledol (use moderately). Boggy acid soils; sphagnum-amended bed.
Annual relative of common motherwort; aerial parts used in TCM (yi mu cao alternative). Self-sows; restricted in some jurisdictions.
Flowering tops historically used for cough and digestive complaints. Self-sows aggressively; considered noxious in some pastures.
Seeds harvested for omega-3 oil and bulking laxative. Cool season annual; sow as soon as soil works. High-oil selections for medicinal use.
Aerial parts used historically as astringent for diarrhea. Highly invasive in wetlands; cultivation banned in many US states. Verify legality.
Silvery-leaved Mediterranean horehound; aerial parts used as bitter cough remedy. Drought tolerant; full sun, sandy soil.
Tetraploid German chamomile bred for elevated bisabolol and chamazulene. Larger flowers than wild type; preferred for tea and oil distillation.
Polish tetraploid chamomile selection with high bisabolol oxide. Picks easily; flowers thicker than wild chamomile.
Aerial parts harvested before flowering as mineral-rich nutritive tea. Deep taproot brings up minerals. Distinct medicinal use from forage cultivation.
Aerial parts contain coumarin; used historically as anticoagulant. Improperly dried hay causes sweet clover disease in livestock. Use cautiously.
Source of menthol-rich essential oil distinct from peppermint. Aerial parts harvested before flowering. Contain runners.
Aerial parts harvested at peak bloom for thymol-rich respiratory tea. North American native bee balm; powdery mildew resistant strains preferred.
Aerial parts used as cold remedy in Oswego Tea tradition. Higher in geraniol than M. fistulosa. Moist soil; tolerates light shade.
Highest thymol of native bee balms; potent antimicrobial. Aerial parts harvested in flower. Sandy well-drained soil, full sun.
Root bark harvested in fall as astringent and circulatory stimulant. Coastal native shrub; salt tolerant; nitrogen fixer.
Aerial parts harvested for vitamin and glucosinolate rich tonic salad. Grow in clean flowing water or saturated wet bed; avoid liver fluke water.
High-nepetalactone selection for human medicinal use as carminative and mild sedative tea. Distinct from cat-attracting cultivars.
Lemon-scented catnip variant; pleasant tea for children. Less attractive to cats; gentler nervine effect than standard catnip.
Seeds pressed for GLA-rich evening primrose oil. Roots edible in year 1; flowers and seed in year 2. Self-sows readily.
Roots harvested year 2+ as diuretic in European pharmacopoeia. Spiny legume; tough taproot. Sandy lean soil.
Roots harvested year 3+ as antispasmodic in European tradition. Distinct medicinal use from ornamental peonies; deep loam.
Petals used as mild sedative tea, especially for children. Lower alkaloid content than P. somniferum; self-sows in disturbed ground.
Source of pharmaceutical opiate alkaloids. Cultivation for medicinal use is controlled or illegal in many jurisdictions; verify legality first.
Root harvested fall year 1 or 2 as low-dose lymphatic herb. Highly toxic in larger amounts; use only with qualified guidance. Self-sows.
Leaves harvested through season for poultice and tea; classic drawing herb. Self-sows; tolerates compacted soil and foot traffic.
Narrow-leaf plantain; aerial parts used as respiratory expectorant. Self-sows; tolerates poor soil.
Aerial parts used as hemostatic and peppery culinary herb. Tolerates wet feet; self-sows in moist disturbed ground.
Rhizomes harvested fall year 2 as strong astringent for diarrhea and bleeding gums. Small yellow-flowered moorland plant; acidic soil.
Aerial parts and roots used as astringent for cramps and diarrhea. Silvery underside of leaves; stoloniferous in moist ground.
Inner bark of small branches harvested fall as cough syrup base. North American native tree; bark contains cyanogenic glycosides, use briefly.
Larger spotted-leaf relative of common lungwort; demulcent respiratory tea. Shade lover; humus-rich moist soil.
Whole plant harvested in spring as topical for hemorrhoids. Invasive in many US states; verify legality. Spring ephemeral.
Aged bark used as stimulant laxative. Bark must be aged 1 year before use to avoid emesis. Invasive in many US states; verify legality.
Petals harvested at peak bloom for European apothecary preparations. Strongly fragrant historic cultivar; retains scent in dried form.
Source of rose otto essential oil and rose water. Harvest blooms in early morning before heat. Bulgarian Kazanlak strain preferred for distillation.
Hips harvested fall for TCM use (ying shi); resolves stagnation. Invasive in many US states; verify legality before planting.
Leaves harvested before flowering as uterine tonic and astringent. Distinct medicinal use from berry harvest; cultivar selection prioritizes leaf yield.
Whole plant harvested in flower; ingredient in Essiac formula. Aggressive spreader on acid soil; deep tap root.
Aerial parts historically used; phototoxic and abortifacient. Use only with qualified guidance; gloves when handling. Restricted in some jurisdictions.
Flowering tops harvested year 2 for sclareol-rich essential oil; nervine and hormonal balancer. Distinct from culinary clary use.
Aerial parts used as wound herb in European tradition. Shade-loving woodland plant; partial to full shade; humus-rich soil.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering as carvacrol-rich digestive and antimicrobial. Subshrub; dry alkaline soil intensifies oil.
Annual aromatic herb; aerial parts used for digestion and bean cookery. Cut before flowering for highest essential oil.
American mad-dog skullcap selected for high baicalin and scutellarin. Aerial parts harvested at flowering as nervine. Moist shade.
European native skullcap relative; aerial parts used as nervine. Tolerates wet feet; pond margin or boggy bed.
Berries harvested late fall from 10+ year plants for prostate-supporting fatty acid extract. Florida sand scrub native; very slow grower.
High-silymarin selection bred for liver-supporting seed extract. Harvest seeds in fall when flower heads fluff. Spiny; gloves recommended.
Rhizome harvested year 3+ in TCM (tu fu ling) for damp-clearing. Climbing vine with thorns; trellis required.
Roots harvested year 4+ as alterative and skin tonic. Climbing vine; tropical only. Steroidal saponins for hormonal balance traditions.
Aerial parts used as nervine and headache remedy in European tradition. Magenta flower spikes; rosette habit; full sun to part shade.
Fuzzy leaves used as poultice for stings and minor wounds. Drought tolerant silvery groundcover.
Whole plant harvested fresh as cooling poultice and salve base. Cool-season weed; self-sows; pick before flowering.
Selected medicinal comfrey for topical bone and skin work. Internal use restricted in many countries due to pyrrolizidine alkaloids.
Aerial parts used as anise-flavored tea in Aztec tradition; calmative and digestive. Treat as annual north of zone 8.
South American tagetes; aerial parts used as nematode suppressant and folk remedy for digestive worms. Tall annual; self-sows in warm zones.
European thyme with chemical races; cherry-thymol selection useful for syrups. Mat-forming; lean soil intensifies essential oil.
Flowers and leaves traditionally used for cough; internal use restricted in many countries due to pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Aggressive spreader.
Inner bark from 10+ year coppice trees used as soothing demulcent. United Plant Savers at-risk; cultivate from seed only; avoid wildcrafting.
Annual nettle used similarly to stinging nettle. Smaller plant; self-sows. Higher stinging potency despite smaller size.
Selection grown for highest mineral content; cut at 12 inches for spring nettle harvest. Distinct cultivation pattern from fiber strain.
Berries harvested for vision-supporting anthocyanins; distinct from blueberry. Acid sphagnum-rich soil; cool moist climate.
Leaves harvested for urinary tract herb arbutin source. Berries also rich in antioxidants. Cold-loving acid bog ericaceous shrub.
Roots harvested fall year 2 from high-valerenic acid selection. Distinct pharmacopoeial strain from ornamental. Sniff test: stronger than typical.
North American native valerian; large edible/medicinal root used by indigenous peoples. Mild sedative; full sun, well-drained meadow.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering as expectorant and skin alterative. Creeping perennial; partial shade tolerant.
Inner bark harvested spring from 3+ year coppice stems as antispasmodic. Distinct medicinal use from ornamental snowball viburnum.
Bark used as uterine antispasmodic; North American native. Distinct medicinal use from V. opulus. Edible blue-black berries.
Aerial parts contain vincamine; used in European medicine for cerebral circulation. Aggressive shade groundcover; invasive in many woodlands.
Flowers and leaves used as lymphatic mover and gentle laxative. Spring ephemeral; spreads by runner; partial shade.
Aerial parts used for skin conditions and respiratory complaints. Self-sows in cool seasons. Edible flowers also.
Berries harvested fall year 2 or 3 for hormonal balancer in Western herbalism. Mediterranean shrub; full sun, drought tolerant.
Bark and berries used as circulatory stimulant and toothache remedy. North American native; sharp thorns. Slow-growing understory tree.
Husks of fruit used in TCM as hua jiao for cold-dispelling and digestive warming. Distinct medicinal use from culinary Sichuan pepper.
Pine cone-shaped inflorescence yields aromatic juice traditionally used as hair rinse and anti-inflammatory. Rhizome also medicinal.

windows.notes: Inoculate hardwood logs late spring

entries.notes: Perennial polypore with immune-supporting polysaccharides; alternative to G. lucidum. Cultivate on hardwood logs in shaded forest setting.

windows.notes: Inoculate dead birch logs

entries.notes: Razor strop fungus; traditional anti-inflammatory tea. Grows on dead birch only; cultivate on weakened or recently fallen birch logs.

windows.notes: Inoculate oak stumps

entries.notes: Polysaccharides studied for immune support; well-known edible. Cultivate via stump inoculation on dying oak.

windows.notes: Inoculate buried oak logs

entries.notes: D-fraction polysaccharide source; strain selected for elevated beta-glucan extraction. Buried log technique; fruits annually on oak.

windows.notes: Inoculate stump or buried logs

entries.notes: Sclerotia used in TCM as damp-draining herb. Cultivation slow; buried hardwood log technique with stump inoculation.

windows.notes: Schedule I in US; verify legality

entries.notes: Cultivation of psilocybin mushrooms is illegal in most jurisdictions. Schedule I federal in US. Entry exists for completeness; verify local law first.
Tall yellow yarrow; similar profile to A. millefolium for wound work. Drought tolerant; full sun.
Higher camphor than English lavender; used historically for headaches and respiratory. Tender Mediterranean species; greenhouse north of zone 7.
Camphoraceous spike lavender oil used for respiratory and muscle work. Higher yield than English lavender; lower-elevation Mediterranean.
High-yield commercial distillation cultivar; oil prized for cleaning and topical infusions. Larger plant than English lavender.
Tender lavender with fern-like leaves; gentler oil profile. Greenhouse north of zone 8. Used in North African folk medicine.
Seeds harvested fall as mucilage-forming demulcent and omega-3 source. Short-day plant; flowers only with shorter days in cool autumn.
Native California chia traditionally used by Chumash. Cool moist winters required; sandy soil; cold germination.
Strong clove-scented basil used in West African and Caribbean folk medicine. Anti-inflammatory leaf tea. Treat as annual north of zone 9.
Less common tulsi variant grown in Hindu temple gardens. Aromatic adaptogen for daily tea. Pinch flowers to extend leaf production.

windows.notes: Inoculate with host Haloxylon roots

entries.notes: Desert root parasite of saxaul; harvested year 5+. Yang tonic in TCM. CITES II protected; cultivate only with licensed host plants.
Bark (he huan pi) and flowers (he huan hua) used in TCM as shen-calming herbs. Small fast-growing tree; can be invasive in mild climates.
Bitter root harvested year 5+; classic European digestive bitter. Cold-stratify seed 8 weeks. Cool moist mountain conditions.
Roots and rhizomes harvested year 3+ as TCM heat-clearing bitter. Distinct species from European G. lutea. Acidic moist soil.
Mat-forming alpine gentian; roots historically used as digestive bitter substitute for G. lutea. Acid scree soil; cool conditions.
Flowers and root used as expectorant in European herbalism. Root harvested fall year 2 for saponin content. Spring ephemeral; partial shade.
Used similarly to cowslip as respiratory herb; taller and looser flower head. Woodland species; humus-rich moist soil.
Aged bark from 3+ year trees used as stimulant laxative. Bark must be aged 1 year before use. Pacific Northwest native; partial shade.
Cold-hardy rosemary selection (to 0F); higher hardiness for medicinal harvest in cooler zones. Strong rosmarinic acid content.
Madelene Hill cold-hardy rosemary; suitable for outdoor cultivation in zone 6 protected sites. Strong rosemary oil for tincture.
Bright yellow yarrow hybrid; medicinal use similar to A. millefolium for wounds and diaphoresis. Drought tolerant; full sun.
Brick-red yarrow strain; same medicinal use as wild yarrow. Holds color longer than Cerise Queen.
Aerial parts harvested at flowering as nervine sedative. Selection bred for elevated flavonoid content. Vine; trellis or fence.
Hardier than P. incarnata; aerial parts used similarly as gentle sedative. Self-sows in mild climates.
Tropical passionflower used in Latin American folk medicine. Distinct fetid scent crushed; vine; tropical only.
Larger-flowered trillium with similar medicinal profile. Wild populations vulnerable; cultivate from seed only; expect 7+ year wait to flowering.
European honeysuckle; flowers used historically as cough remedy. Climbing vine; fragrant blooms. Distinct from L. japonica jin yin hua.
Aerial parts harvested year 2 in flower as bitter digestive tonic. Small pink-flowered biennial; sandy lean soil.
Whole flowering plant harvested year 2 as digestive bitter and antimalarial in Ayurveda. Cool Himalayan species; struggles in heat.
Rhizome harvested year 2+ as Ayurvedic hepatoprotective. CITES II protected; cultivate to relieve wild pressure. Cold alpine.
Bark and roots harvested year 4+ as African ethnobotanical source of reserpine-type alkaloids. Restricted; tropical only.
Inner bark from 5+ year vine harvested for immune-supporting alkaloids. Amazonian woody climber; tropical only; large trellis required.
Hooked stems harvested year 3+ in TCM as liver wind-clearing herb. Climbing vine; subtropical only.
Rajasthan Marwadi strain prized for fatter cluster of tuberous roots. Female reproductive tonic in Ayurveda. Sandy soil, trellis vine.
Roots harvested fall year 1 as Ayurvedic rasayana. White-flowered lily relative; tropical; sandy loam, monsoon irrigation pattern.
Yellow-flowered groundcover used as bhringraj alternative in southern India for hair tonic. Invasive in tropical areas; verify legality.
Succulent leaves used in Ayurveda for kidney stones (patharchatta) and topical use. Propagates from leaf margin plantlets; greenhouse north of zone 9.
PKM-1 or PKM-2 selections bred for high leaf yield. Leaves harvested green for nutritive powder. Coppice annually; tropical fast grower.
entries.source: Indian Council of Agricultural Research bulletin

entries.notes: Ethiopian cabbage tree; larger leaves than M. oleifera. Used as staple food and traditional medicine in East Africa.
Leaves, bark, and seed oil used across Ayurveda as antimicrobial and pest deterrent. Tropical evergreen tree; greenhouse north of zone 9.
Whole plant used in Ayurveda for digestive and respiratory conditions. Common tropical roadside weed; self-sows in warm climates.
Latex used externally only in Ayurveda; highly toxic internally. Drought tolerant shrub of arid regions. Topical use only.
Highly toxic tropane plant used externally only in Ayurveda. Restricted or banned in many jurisdictions; verify legality before planting.
Rhizome harvested year 3+ as TCM heat- and damp-clearing herb. Climbing vine without thorns; partial shade.
Leaves harvested for digestive and nervine tea. Drop leaves in cold; greenhouse north of zone 8. Citral-rich essential oil.
Lemon-scented Brazilian medicinal mint relative used as sedative and digestive tea. Aromatic shrub; tropical only.
Leaves harvested year 4+ for stimulating xanthine-rich tea. South American native; subtropical only. Distinct from yerba santa.
Native caffeine-bearing holly used by southeastern indigenous peoples as black drink. Only caffeine-containing plant native to North America.
Amazonian caffeine-bearing holly; leaves harvested year 4+ for ceremonial morning tea. Tropical only; partial shade tolerant.
Roots harvested year 1 as source of forskolin compound. Indian Ayurvedic herb; sandy soil; greenhouse north of zone 9.
Tubers used in Ayurveda for digestion and TCM as xiang fu for qi stagnation. Aggressive weed in agriculture; isolate cultivation.

entries.notes: Aquatic dock species. Young leaves edible cooked (oxalic acid; rotate). Mineral accumulator for wet permaculture sites.

windows.notes: Tidal marsh or brackish pond margin

entries.notes: Salt-marsh sedge. Edible tubers and seeds; traditional Native American food crop. Brackish water tolerant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Plants for a Future

windows.notes: Plant in shallow pond margin or wet meadow spring

entries.notes: Native rush. Edible young shoots and rhizomes. Wetland restoration plant; basket weaving stems.

windows.notes: Rhizome planting in pond margin spring

entries.notes: Aromatic rhizome (vacha) used medicinally. Triploid form preferred; diploid contains beta-asarone. Use cautiously.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds catalog; Plants for a Future

windows.notes: Pond margin shallow water spring planting

entries.notes: Edible seeds (nutty, roasted) and young leaves (cooked). Native wetland perennial. Purple flower spikes pollinator value.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Samuel Thayer The Forager's Harvest

windows.notes: Direct sow spring in wet marshy soil

entries.notes: Wetland progenitor of cultivated celery. Strong celery flavor; leaves and stems. Marsh-edge permaculture herb.
entries.source: Plants for a Future; Royal Horticultural Society

entries.notes: Cascade and Rocky Mountain subalpine deciduous shrub, acidic well-drained soil, partial shade. Slow to fruit (3-5 years). Traditional food of Salish, Nez Perce; ethical harvest required for wild plants, cultivation preferred.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service Pacific Northwest Research Station

entries.notes: PNW alpine meadow groundcover blueberry, sweet bluish fruit. Acidic peat soil, full sun at elevation. Slow garden subject; protect from drought.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension native plant guide

entries.notes: Coastal PNW and boreal moist forest huckleberry; tart blue berries used by Tlingit, Haida. Acidic humus, dappled shade. Traditional food, cultivation preferred.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Low mat-forming huckleberry of subalpine meadows and bogs. Sweet blue berries; valued by Indigenous gatherers. Needs cool moist acid soil.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Low evergreen understory shrub of PNW Douglas-fir forests. Tart blue berries best for jelly. Shade-tolerant, drought tolerant once established.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: Low groundcover form, intermountain west. Tart bluish berries for jelly or syrup. Hardier than M. aquifolium; tolerates dry shade.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Colorado State University Extension

entries.notes: PNW native blackberry, smaller and sweeter than invasive Himalayan. Trailing canes need trellis. Parent of loganberry, marionberry, boysenberry.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: Arctic and boreal bog dioecious bramble; amber berries highly prized. Needs acidic peat, cool summers. Dioecious, plant both sexes.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Circumboreal low herbaceous raspberry; intensely aromatic pink fruit. Finnish breeding produced 'Mesma', 'Pima' cultivars. Acid humus, cool.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) trial reports

entries.notes: Western black raspberry, glaucous canes, deep purple-black fruit. Ancestor of 'Munger'. Tip-layer to propagate; biennial canes.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: PNW understory groundcover bramble, soft red berries in twos. Modest yield, mostly forage and woodland edge ornament.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Multi-stemmed suckering form, heavy crops of sweet blue-purple berries. Prairie heritage cultivar, excellent for hedgerows.
entries.source: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada cultivar descriptor; University of Saskatchewan fruit program

entries.notes: Late-ripening Saskatchewan cultivar, large clusters of 15+ berries, slightly sweeter than Smoky. Less suckering.
entries.source: University of Saskatchewan fruit program; Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada

entries.notes: Mid-season, mild sweet flavor, moderate yields. Compact habit suits home plantings; light suckering.
entries.source: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Large fruit (up to 17mm), uniform ripening, commercial favorite. Selected from Thiessen seedlings.
Historic 1870s heritage selection, mild flavor, smaller fruit. Heavy producer over long ripening window.
entries.source: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Eastern woodland thicket-forming serviceberry, prefers moist sites. Smaller fruit than Saskatoon; good for wildlife and small jams.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Maine Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Larger bulb than C. quamash, deeper blue flowers. Traditional pit-cooked food of PNW peoples. Plant bulbs in fall, moist meadow conditions.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: PNW dry meadow native onion, pink starburst umbels. Mild garlicky bulbs, traditional food. Plant in fall, dry summer dormancy.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Burke Museum ethnobotany records

entries.notes: Mediterranean origin but naturalized in PNW; aggressive in mild climates. Triangular stems, mild garlic flavor; all parts edible. Treat as invasive in coastal CA, OR.
entries.source: Oregon Department of Agriculture noxious weed profile; UC Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Coastal redwood and Douglas-fir understory shamrock-leaved groundcover. Tart lemony leaves, eat in moderation due to oxalates. Deep shade.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Northeastern and Appalachian conifer forest understory. Tart edible leaves and pink-veined flowers; oxalate caution. Cool moist shade.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: CAUTION: needles, seeds, bark all highly toxic; ONLY the red fleshy aril (without seed) is safe. PNW conifer; source of paclitaxel cancer drug. Slow-growing.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service Pacific Northwest Research Station

entries.notes: Boreal forest groundcover dogwood with bright red berry clusters. Mild flavor, traditional pudding ingredient. Cool acid humus, partial shade.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Maine Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: PNW understory tree, edible flower bracts and red berry clusters (cooked). Mainly ornamental; berries astringent raw. Anthracnose-sensitive.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: Circumboreal sphagnum bog cranberry, smaller than commercial V. macrocarpon but similar tart flavor. Needs wet acidic peat, full sun.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Wisconsin Cranberry Board

entries.notes: Circumpolar low evergreen heath shrub, black juicy berries. Bland to mildly sweet; traditional Inuit food, often mixed with seal oil. Acidic peat.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: PNW spiny gooseberry, dark purple berries, sweet when ripe. Streambank and woodland edge. Parent of some cultivated gooseberries.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: PNW deciduous shrub, pink-red flowers in early spring, blue-black berries with whitish bloom. Berries bland but edible; mainly ornamental and pollinator food.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: Sprawling montane currant, glandular black berries. Tart edible; modest yield, mostly wildlife forage.
PNW streambank currant, pungent foliage but edible blue-black berries with white bloom. Traditional food of coastal First Nations; best cooked.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Royal BC Museum ethnobotany records

entries.notes: PNW twining vine with tubular orange flowers (edible nectar). Berries reported edible by some sources but generally not eaten; toxicity uncertain. Pollinator plant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: PNW dry forest shrub, dense cream flower plumes. Seeds traditionally eaten by Salish peoples; wood prized for digging sticks and tools.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Burke Museum ethnobotany records

entries.notes: PNW wetland shrub, pink flower spikes. Leaves and flowers used for traditional tea; not for fruit. Wet sites, full sun.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: CAUTION: raw seeds and stems toxic; cooked deseeded berries used by PNW peoples. Bright red clusters. Differs from blue/black elders, more toxic raw.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: CAUTION: sap is phototoxic (furanocoumarins); handle with gloves long sleeves. Peeled young stems traditional PNW food. Do not confuse with giant hogweed (H. mantegazzianum).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Alaska Native Knowledge Network

entries.notes: Boreal bog evergreen shrub; leaves brewed as traditional tea. Use small amounts; contains ledol. Formerly Ledum groenlandicum.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Eurasian and arctic North American counterpart; stronger flavor. Brew sparingly. Formerly Ledum palustre.
Circumboreal evergreen mat-forming groundcover. Mealy red berries, bland but edible; leaves used medicinally for urinary tract. Tolerates poor sandy soils.
Circumboreal bog and tundra blueberry, glaucous blue fruit. Traditional food in Scandinavia, Russia, Alaska. Cool acidic peat.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Boreal forest lowbush blueberry, hairy leaves. Sweet blue fruit, important traditional food of Cree, Anishinaabe.
1959 Michigan selection by Corwin Davis. Greenish-yellow fruit, mild custard flavor, moderate seed count. Hardy and early ripening.
entries.source: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Heavy producer, large fruit, mild sweet flavor. Selected from California planting; reliable cropper in mid-Atlantic.
entries.source: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Canadian selection, large yellow fruit, few seeds, banana-mango flavor. Early ripening, productive in shorter seasons.
entries.source: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Indiana selection, large fruit (up to 1 lb), orange flesh, rich tropical flavor. Moderate seed count.
entries.source: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Late-ripening selection, large yellow fruit, sweet custard flavor. Extends harvest window into late September.
entries.source: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Illinois selection, medium-large fruit, yellow flesh, distinct banana flavor. Reliable mid-season producer.
entries.source: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Maryland heirloom, medium fruit, sweet rich custard flavor. Heavy bearer once established.
entries.source: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Indiana selection, medium orange fruit, rich sweet flavor, ripens late. Productive self-fruitful tree (but cross-pollination boosts yield).
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor; University of Kentucky Extension

entries.notes: Early-ripening Indiana selection, medium fruit, high sugar. Good for short-season Midwest sites.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Large fruit, rich flavor, late ripening. Selected in Indiana, popular with persimmon enthusiasts.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Iowa selection, medium fruit, very productive, cold hardy. Reliable cropper north of typical persimmon range.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Medium-large fruit, parthenocarpic (seedless when no pollinator). Mid-season, rich flavor.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Large fruit, dependably productive, late season. One of the most widely planted American persimmons.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor; Kentucky State University Extension

entries.notes: Large fruit (up to 2 inches), sweet rich flavor, productive. Indiana selection, late ripening.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Historic 1880 Illinois heirloom, early ripening, small-medium golden fruit. Parent of many later cultivars.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor; Kentucky State University Extension

entries.notes: Late-season counterpart, extends harvest into October. Medium golden fruit, rich flavor.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Indiana selection, exceptionally rich complex flavor, medium fruit. Connoisseur favorite, mid-season.
entries.source: Indiana Nut Growers Association cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Ukrainian hybrid (kaki x virginiana) from Nikita Botanical Gardens. Large 2-inch sweet fruit, cold hardier than pure kaki. Self-fertile.
entries.source: Kentucky State University Pawpaw and Persimmon Program; Cornell Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: CAUTION: all parts EXCEPT fully ripe yellow fruit are toxic. Eastern woodland colony-forming herb. Ripe golden fruit makes tart jelly.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Kentucky Extension

entries.notes: Larger-tubered selection from LSU Apios breeding program (William Blackmon). Vining legume with edible protein-rich tubers, traditional food of Eastern Woodland peoples.
entries.source: Louisiana State University AgCenter Apios breeding program; USDA NRCS

entries.notes: LSU-bred improved cultivars produce larger tubers in single season vs wild type's 2-3 year cycle. Plant on trellis or fence.
entries.source: Louisiana State University AgCenter Apios breeding program

entries.notes: Eastern woodland herbaceous perennial, aromatic root used medicinally; berries edible cooked. Tall (4-6 ft) shaded gardens.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; United Plant Savers

entries.notes: Northern hardwood forest groundcover, aromatic rhizome used in root beer flavoring. Dark blue berries edible but bland.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Maine Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Eastern woodland aromatic tree, mitten-shaped leaves dried for file powder (gumbo thickener). Root beer flavoring; FDA restricts safrole oil. Suckers freely.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Late winter blooming witch hazel of Ozark streams. Bark distilled for astringent; primarily medicinal use. Pollinator plant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Missouri Department of Conservation

entries.notes: Sweet acorns (low tannin among oaks); still requires leaching for human food. Traditional food of Eastern Woodland and Cherokee peoples. 15-20 years to acorn bearing.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Plains and Midwest oak with massive fringe-cupped acorns. Moderate tannin; cold-leach for flour. Traditional food of Plains peoples.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: HIGH tannin acorns; require extensive cold-water leaching for food use. Faster growing than white oak. Mainly for wildlife and timber.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: American Chestnut Foundation B3F3 backcross and Darling 58 transgenic lines bred for chestnut blight resistance. Plant only in approved restoration programs.
entries.source: American Chestnut Foundation breeding program reports; SUNY ESF transgenic research

entries.notes: Ozark Mountain endemic, small sweet single-nutted burs. Blight-decimated; Ozark Chinquapin Foundation breeds for resistance.
entries.source: Ozark Chinquapin Foundation breeding program; USDA NRCS

entries.notes: Largest hickory nuts, sweet kernels, very hard shell. Bottomland species; tolerates wet sites. Slow to bear (15+ years from seed).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Iowa State University Extension

entries.notes: Bitter inedible nuts (sulfur compounds); used historically for lamp oil. Mainly timber and wildlife value. Often used as rootstock for grafted pecan.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Eastern white walnut, sweet oily kernels, easier to crack than black walnut. Threatened by butternut canker; seek resistant selections.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service Northern Research Station

entries.notes: Appalachian and Eastern dry-site lowbush blueberry. Smaller fruit than V. angustifolium but heat-tolerant. Acidic well-drained soil.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Penn State Extension

entries.notes: Eastern upland Vaccinium with bell flowers and tart green-to-purple berries. Best for jams; raw flavor variable. Drought tolerant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Florida IFAS Extension

entries.notes: Eastern wetland-edge chokeberry, bright red persistent fruit. Astringent raw, good for syrups, jellies, juice blends. Stunning fall color.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Connecticut Extension

entries.notes: Natural hybrid of A. melanocarpa and A. arbutifolia. Dark purple fruit, intermediate astringency. Good wildlife shrub.
PNW and Rocky Mountain hawthorn, deep purple-black haws. Sweet edible fruit; traditional food of Salish, Nez Perce. Sharp thorns.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Oregon State University Extension

entries.notes: Northern Plains and boreal hawthorn, bright red-orange haws. Mealy sweet flesh; edible fresh or in preserves.
Midwest and Northeast hawthorn with juicy red haws, considered among the better-eating native hawthorns. Pectin-rich for jelly.
Eastern woodland native mulberry, deep purple-red sweet fruit. Threatened by hybridization with introduced M. alba. Plant pure red mulberry from local seed sources.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Kentucky Extension

entries.notes: Southern heirloom selection, very long ripening window (June through August). Sweet small-to-medium black fruit, light seasoning of seeds.
entries.source: Just Fruits and Exotics cultivar descriptor; Stark Bro's heritage notes

entries.notes: Edible pink flowers harvested early spring before leaf-out, tangy pea-like flavor for salads. Young seed pods cookable. Understory tree.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Forest Service Eastern Region tree guide

entries.notes: Young leaves edible (mild, lettuce-like), flowers brewed for tea, source of premium honey. Important nectar tree of Eastern forests.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Triangular sweet beechnuts traditional food of Eastern Woodland peoples. Masting tree (heavy crops every 2-8 years). Beech leaf disease emerging threat.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service Northern Research Station

entries.notes: Eastern aquatic plant; seeds (chinquapin nut) and rhizomes traditional food of many tribes. Yellow flowers. Needs still freshwater 2-5 ft deep.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Indigenous foodways research, University of Arkansas

entries.notes: CAUTION: raw plant contains protoanemonin (toxic); MUST be boiled in 2-3 changes of water. Cooked young leaves traditional spring green. Wetland soil.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Minnesota Extension

entries.notes: Luther Burbank's 1911 thornless selection. Large smooth pads (nopales) and sweet red fruit (tunas). May develop glochids in stress; handle with care.
entries.source: USDA GRIN germplasm descriptor; UC Davis cactus pear program

entries.notes: Sonoran Desert species, purple pads especially in winter cold stress. Edible fruit and young pads (requires glochid removal). Ornamental and edible.
entries.source: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension; Desert Botanical Garden

entries.notes: Mexican cultivar producing tender nopal pads, less mucilage when cooked. Productive in arid conditions; commercial nopal source.
entries.source: INIFAP Mexico cactus pear research; UC Davis cactus program

entries.notes: Mexican commercial cultivar, sweet large yellow-orange tunas. Productive in arid zones, drought tolerant.
Sprawling Texas/SW native, deep purple-red tunas. Traditional Tohono O'odham food. Cold-hardier than O. ficus-indica.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

entries.notes: Chihuahuan Desert species, long black spines on bluish pads. Bright red-purple tunas, sweet. Striking ornamental and edible.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Desert Botanical Garden

entries.notes: Widespread SW and Great Basin sprawling form. Reddish-purple tunas, traditional food. Cold-hardy to zone 5 in dry soils.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Arizona Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Northern Plains and Rocky Mountain prickly pear, very cold-hardy (zone 3). Small dry fruit; traditional food, often eaten dried. Glochid removal required.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Colorado State University Extension

entries.notes: Eastern North America's only native prickly pear; low spreading form. Sweet red tunas; cold-hardy. Tolerates moist sandy soils.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Penn State Extension

entries.notes: Densely spined Sonoran cholla; ciolim (flower buds) traditional Tohono O'odham food after careful spine removal and pit-roasting. Ethical wild harvest only.
entries.source: Tohono O'odham Community Action ethnobotany; University of Arizona Extension

entries.notes: Sonoran Desert branched cholla, multicolored stem segments. Flower buds traditional food; remove spines/glochids by tumbling. Ethical harvest required.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Desert Botanical Garden

entries.notes: Sonoran Desert tree; sweet pods ground into mesquite flour. Traditional staple of Tohono O'odham, Akimel O'odham. Drought-deep-rooted.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; San Xavier Co-op Farm seed bank

entries.notes: Cold-hardy agave of Mogollon Rim. Heart (piña) traditional pit-roasted food of Apache, used for mescal. Monocarpic (dies after flowering).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Arizona Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: SE Arizona and Sonora highland agave, critical lesser long-nosed bat nectar source. Heart traditional Apache food. Slow to maturity (15-25 years).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; US Fish and Wildlife Service bat-agave reports

entries.notes: Central Mexican highland agave used for aguamiel and traditional pulque fermentation. Massive rosettes; tap before flowering bolt.
entries.source: INIFAP Mexico agave research; UC Davis viticulture and enology agave program

entries.notes: Sonoran and Mojave Desert agave, traditional Cahuilla and Kumeyaay food. Pit-roasted heart, flower stalks roasted. Very drought tolerant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; UC Riverside Botanic Gardens

entries.notes: Cold-hardiest American agave, Great Basin and Mojave canyon walls. Traditional Southern Paiute and Hualapai food. Very slow growing.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Utah State University Extension

entries.notes: Heritage black-seeded tepary from Oaxaca region. Extreme drought tolerance, deep nutty flavor. Heat-loving; do not overwater.
entries.source: Native Seeds/SEARCH seed bank descriptor; USDA GRIN

entries.notes: Yaqui (Yoeme) tepary, small tan-streaked seeds, sweet flavor. Traditional food of Yaqui people of Sonora/Arizona.
Pueblo of San Felipe heritage tepary, mottled brown-tan seeds. Adapted to Rio Grande valley conditions, late-summer monsoon.
Wild-collected Sonoran tepary from Pinacate region. Small seeds, exceptional drought adaptation. Early genetic source for breeders.
Hopi heritage cushaw, striped tan and green fruit. Dry-farmed in arid Southwest by Pueblo peoples for centuries. Drought-resilient long vines.
entries.source: Native Seeds/SEARCH seed bank descriptor; Seed Savers Exchange yearbook

entries.notes: CAUTION: bitter cucurbitacins make flesh inedible. Seeds traditionally roasted and eaten in moderation. Drought-tolerant Sonoran perennial gourd.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Desert Botanical Garden

entries.notes: Massive taproot perennial gourd of SW and Plains. Bitter flesh inedible; seeds rich in oil and protein. Research crop for arid land oilseed.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Arizona arid land research

entries.notes: Great Basin desert onion, small white-pink umbels. Traditional Paiute and Shoshone food, harvested in spring. Plant in fall for spring emergence.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Nevada Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Western hackberry of canyon and riparian zones. Sweet date-like berries, traditional food of Apache, Yavapai. Drought-tolerant once established.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Arizona Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Large fleshy fruits eaten fresh or dried; traditional Pueblo, Apache food. Roots saponin source for soap. Pollinated by yucca moth.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Native Seeds/SEARCH

entries.notes: Sonoran Desert keystone cactus; ripe fruit harvested with kuibit pole, traditional Tohono O'odham new year ceremony. ETHICAL WILD HARVEST ONLY by tribal members; cultivation slow.
entries.source: Tohono O'odham Community Action; Saguaro National Park ethnobotany

entries.notes: Sonoran cactus, sweet red pitaya fruit (pitahaya dulce). Traditional Seri (Comcaac) and Tohono O'odham food. Slow growing; protect from frost.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Native Seeds/SEARCH

entries.notes: Yellow tart fruit edible fresh or candied; seeds ground for porridge. Traditional Sonoran Desert food. Flesh emergency water source (myth oversold; mildly toxic raw).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Desert Botanical Garden

entries.notes: Baja California giant columnar cactus, ripe fruit traditional Seri (Comcaac) food. World's largest cactus. Extremely slow to first fruit.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Native Seeds/SEARCH

entries.notes: Whip-like Chihuahuan/Sonoran shrub; tubular orange-red flowers steeped for tart hummingbird-pollinator tea. Wand cuttings root easily into living fence.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Arizona Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Boreal and Rocky Mountain shrub. Tart red berries traditional whipped 'sxusem' (Indian ice cream) of Interior Salish, Dene. Nitrogen-fixer.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Royal BC Museum ethnobotany records

entries.notes: Thicket-forming native plum, red-blushed fruit good for jelly. Excellent wildlife and pollinator shrub. Suckers freely; useful as windbreak.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Iowa State University Extension

entries.notes: Single-trunked Texas/southern Plains plum, deep purple-red fruit, tart-sweet. Excellent for jelly, baking. Non-suckering.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

entries.notes: Northern hardy plum, orange-red oval fruit. Parent of many cold-hardy plum hybrids. Suckers moderately; thicket habit.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada

entries.notes: Great Plains low shrub-cherry, sweet purple-black fruit. Drought tolerant; used as dwarfing rootstock and parent of cherry-plum hybrids.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; South Dakota State University Extension

entries.notes: Cold-hardiest American grape. Small tart blue fruit good for jelly. Critical rootstock source for cold-climate viticulture. Phylloxera resistant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Cornell Grape Breeding Program

entries.notes: Ozark and southern Plains streambank grape. Small intense flavored black fruit. Important phylloxera-resistant rootstock species.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Missouri Grape Program

entries.notes: Eastern woodland native grape, parent of Norton wine grape. Black juicy fruit ripens late summer. Disease-resistant in humid East.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Missouri Grape Program

entries.notes: Ozark glade endemic, the only yellow-flowered Echinacea. Roots used like E. angustifolia. Slow to mature; harvest roots in year 3.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; United Plant Savers

entries.notes: Plains liatris with edible starchy corms; traditional food of Lakota, Cheyenne. Best harvested second year. Drought-tolerant prairie species.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Lakota Foods ethnobotany research

entries.notes: Great Plains yucca, edible flowers and immature pods (cook to remove bitter saponins). Roots traditional soap source. Cold-hardy to zone 3.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; South Dakota State University Extension

entries.notes: Eastern coastal plain yucca with edible white flowers (lightly cooked). Curly leaf fibers traditional cordage. Hardier than southwestern yuccas.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Florida IFAS Extension

entries.notes: CAUTION: must be cooked in 2-3 changes of boiling water; raw plant toxic (cardiac glycosides). Immature pods, young shoots, flower buds traditional food. Critical monarch host.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Xerces Society

entries.notes: Great Plains native onion with fiber-coated bulbs, white star umbels. Strong onion flavor; traditional Lakota, Blackfeet food.
Southern Plains and Texas wild onion, pink-purple umbels. Mild garlic flavor; traditional food. Plant bulbs in fall for spring emergence.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center

entries.notes: Eastern and Central US wild onion with bulblets in umbel. Bulbs and greens edible, strong onion-garlic flavor. Aggressive in lawns.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Minnesota Extension

entries.notes: Pacific Northwest and Rocky Mountain dry-meadow species. Roots traditional staple of Salish, Nez Perce, Bitterroot Salish. Harvest in early spring before bloom; peel inner core. Dies back midsummer.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes ethnobotany

entries.notes: Sego lily of Great Basin. Traditional Mormon pioneer survival food; State flower of Utah. Bulbs sweet-nutty roasted. Ethical harvest required; cultivate from seed.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Utah State University Extension

entries.notes: Lower-sugar sap than sugar maple but tappable; traditional Plains Indigenous syrup source. Fast-growing pioneer tree. Short-lived (60-80 years).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Minnesota Extension

entries.notes: Midwest and Plains hackberry. Small sweet date-like berries with hard seed; eaten whole crushed. Tough urban tree; tolerates drought, alkaline soil.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Morton Arboretum

entries.notes: Self-fertile bronze muscadine, 1970 North Carolina release. Heavy producer, good for juice and wine. Industry workhorse cultivar.
entries.source: North Carolina State University Muscadine Breeding Program; University of Georgia Extension

entries.notes: Self-fertile bronze muscadine, productive late-ripener. Sweet thick skin; good for fresh eating and wine.
entries.source: North Carolina State University Muscadine Breeding Program

entries.notes: Self-fertile bronze muscadine from Mississippi. Medium-large fruit, sweet, good fresh and processed.
entries.source: Mississippi State University Extension; University of Georgia Extension

entries.notes: Self-fertile black muscadine, large fruit, very sweet. Reliable home garden producer with attractive dark color.
entries.source: North Carolina State University Muscadine Breeding Program

entries.notes: Self-fertile dark purple muscadine, classic wine grape. 1971 NC release; standard for red muscadine wine.
entries.source: North Carolina State University Muscadine Breeding Program

entries.notes: Self-fertile black muscadine, late ripening, juice-quality. Used in commercial Southern wine production.
entries.source: University of Georgia Extension Muscadine guide

entries.notes: Historic 1750s North Carolina heritage bronze muscadine, the first named American grape cultivar. Female (needs male pollinizer). Iconic Southern fruit.
entries.source: North Carolina State University Muscadine Breeding Program; USDA GRIN

entries.notes: Self-fertile bronze, large early-ripening fruit, edible skin. Productive home garden variety.
entries.source: University of Georgia Extension Muscadine guide

entries.notes: Self-fertile bronze, very early ripening, good for fresh market. Florida-adapted, high yield potential.
entries.source: University of Florida IFAS Extension; University of Georgia Extension

entries.notes: Self-fertile bronze, productive juice and wine grape. Florida origin, performs well in deep south.
Self-fertile black muscadine, large early fruit, classic Southern home garden choice. Released by USDA Tifton.
entries.source: USDA-ARS Tifton; University of Georgia Extension

entries.notes: Female bronze muscadine (needs pollinizer), very large pink-bronze fruit. Distinctive fresh-eating variety.
entries.source: University of Georgia Extension Muscadine guide

entries.notes: Female black muscadine, very large fruit (>1 inch), sweet rich flavor. Fresh-market favorite; needs male pollinizer.
entries.source: University of Florida IFAS Extension; Ison's Nursery descriptor

entries.notes: Female black muscadine, large sweet fruit. Companion to bronze Fry; both need male pollinizer.
entries.source: University of Georgia Extension Muscadine guide

entries.notes: Female bronze muscadine, very sweet large fruit, high sugar content. Fresh-market specialty cultivar.
entries.source: University of Georgia Extension Muscadine guide

entries.notes: Self-fertile black muscadine, large fruit, sweet. Newer USDA-ARS release, reliable cropper.
entries.source: USDA-ARS Tifton; University of Georgia Extension

entries.notes: Heavy-bearing mayhaw selection, medium-large red fruit. Classic Southern jelly mayhaw; productive in wet sites.
entries.source: Louisiana State University AgCenter mayhaw program; University of Georgia Extension

entries.notes: Louisiana selection, large bright red fruit, classic jelly mayhaw flavor. Productive, disease-resistant.
entries.source: Louisiana State University AgCenter mayhaw program

entries.notes: Heavy producer with dense spur clusters, very productive. Medium fruit, classic mayhaw jelly quality.
entries.source: University of Georgia Extension; Louisiana State University AgCenter

entries.notes: Texas selection, large bright red mayhaw fruit. Productive, well-suited to Gulf Coast wet sites.
entries.source: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension mayhaw guide

entries.notes: Large bright red fruit selection. Common in Louisiana and East Texas commercial mayhaw orchards.
entries.source: Louisiana State University AgCenter mayhaw program

entries.notes: Vigorous selection, medium-large red fruit, productive. Wet-tolerant Gulf Coast mayhaw.
entries.source: Louisiana State University AgCenter mayhaw program

entries.notes: Western Gulf Coast mayhaw species, slightly different leaf shape from C. aestivalis. Fruit equivalent for jelly. Tolerates poorly-drained sites.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Louisiana State University AgCenter

entries.notes: Asian relative naturalized in US gardens. Bright violet berry clusters; edible but mild, mostly ornamental. Leaves repel mosquitoes (callicarpenal).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Missouri Botanical Garden
