entries.notes: Heavy berry-producing yaupon selection. Leaves brewed as North America's only native caffeinated tea (cassina/asi). Roast leaves for full flavor.
entries.source: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension; University of Florida IFAS Extension

entries.notes: Narrow columnar male yaupon selection. Leaves harvest-ready year-round for traditional caffeinated tea. No berries (male clone).
Weeping form female yaupon, abundant berries, leaves for tea. Ornamental + edible. Native of SE US sandhills.
Southern greenbrier vine; young shoots edible like asparagus. Aggressive thorny climber, considered a weed by most but a wild green by foragers.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Florida IFAS Extension

entries.notes: Eastern woodland greenbrier. Young shoots tender wild green, asparagus-flavored. Roots starch source for traditional 'red root' beverage.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Kentucky Extension

entries.notes: SE coastal plain evergreen greenbrier. Young shoots edible; substantial starchy rhizomes traditionally processed as flour.
Low-growing SE greenbrier, less thorny. Tender young shoots and red berries edible; root historically used for sarsaparilla flavoring.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Florida IFAS Extension

entries.notes: Small Texas Hill Country tree, black 1-inch fruit when ripe, sweet pulp. Dioecious; needs male and female. Drought-tolerant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

entries.notes: South Florida and Caribbean wetland Annona. Yellow-green fruit edible but watery; mostly used for jam. Critical Everglades species. Frost-sensitive.
entries.source: University of Florida IFAS Extension; USDA NRCS plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Very large orange-yellow fruit, balanced sweet-tart. California-bred, popular for fresh eating.
entries.source: California Rare Fruit Growers cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Florida-bred yellow-fleshed loquat, large fruit, productive. Adapted to humid Gulf Coast conditions.
Japanese classic, very large yellow-orange fruit, firm flesh. Late-season, holds well on tree.
entries.source: California Rare Fruit Growers cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Very early ripening (December in mild winter areas, hence name). Yellow-orange fruit, sweet, productive.
entries.source: California Rare Fruit Growers cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: Circumboreal arctic-alpine bunchberry analog, red berry clusters. Edible mild flavor. Cool acid peat, full sun in tundra to partial shade in taiga.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Naturalized in N North America. Bright orange-red berries traditionally made into Scandinavian rowan jelly (must cook to neutralize parasorbic acid).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Minnesota Extension

entries.notes: Northeastern and Appalachian native mountain ash. Bright red berry clusters; tart, must be cooked. Best after frost. Important wildlife food.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Maine Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Larger fruit than S. americana, brighter scarlet color, more ornamental. Edible cooked; best after first frost sweetens. Boreal forest tree.
Boreal Viburnum, tart red-orange fruit, single flat seed. Traditional food of Athabaskan, Inuit peoples; cooked into pemmican or jelly.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Boreal currant, black berries, pungent foliage. Edible but strong flavor; better cooked. Cool moist sites.
Circumboreal wet-site currant, bright red translucent fruit. Tart but pleasant; jelly-grade. Traditional Boreal Indigenous food.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Boreal currant with skunky foliage but mild red fruit. Edible, mainly for jam after deseeding. Cool moist forest understory.
Boreal bog spruce, young spring tips harvested for tea, syrup, or beer. High vitamin C. Slow growing; widespread northern wood.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Canadian Forest Service

entries.notes: Boreal upland spruce; spring tips traditional Indigenous tea (Sitka, Cree). Citrusy flavor, very high vitamin C. Harvest 1-2 inches per branch tip.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Rocky Mountain subalpine spruce. Bright green spring tips for tea and syrup; bright citrus-resin flavor. Harvest sustainably (one tip per branch tier).
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Western and boreal pine. Cambium (inner bark) traditional food of Salish, Nlaka'pamux, harvested in spring. Caution: bark harvest can kill tree, ethical practices essential.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Royal BC Museum ethnobotany

entries.notes: Deciduous boreal conifer. Soft spring needle clusters edible (mild lemon flavor); inner bark and gum traditional Indigenous food and medicine. Wet sites.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Alaska Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: Sap tapped in early spring (after maples, before leaf-out). Boil to birch syrup at 100:1 ratio (vs 40:1 maple). Traditional food across Boreal.
entries.source: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension; Cornell Maple Program birch trial

entries.notes: Tappable for syrup but earlier bud break shortens season vs sugar maple. About 60:1 sap-to-syrup. Widespread Eastern tree.
entries.source: Cornell Cooperative Extension Maple Program; University of Vermont Proctor Maple Research Center

entries.notes: Bright red fall color selection. Vigorous, sugar-tappable when mature (25+ year tap-size). Shade tree first, syrup second.
entries.source: Morton Arboretum cultivar descriptor; J. Frank Schmidt and Son nursery

entries.notes: Heat and drought-tolerant sugar maple from Caddo County Oklahoma. Better suited to Southern Plains than typical sugar maple. Tappable.
entries.source: Oklahoma State University Extension; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: Dense crown, exceptional fall color, drought-tolerant sugar maple selection. Tappable when mature.
Midwest sugar maple relative; tapped equivalently for syrup. Tolerates wetter sites than A. saccharum. Sometimes treated as subspecies.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Cornell Maple Program

entries.notes: North America's most widespread tree. Cambium (inner bark) traditional spring food of Plains and Boreal peoples; also famine food. Catkins edible cooked.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; USDA Forest Service

entries.notes: European species widely planted in N America. Young leaves mild salad green, flowers brewed for relaxing tea. Premium honey source.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Royal Horticultural Society

entries.notes: SE thicket-forming small plum, deep red-yellow fruit. Traditional food of Chickasaw, Choctaw, widely planted by Indigenous trade. Pollinator-rich early bloom.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Florida IFAS Extension

entries.notes: Multiplying shallot of Tohono O'odham origin, named for I'itoi deity. Heat- and drought-tolerant; mild pink-skinned bulbs and greens. Divide and replant.
entries.source: Native Seeds/SEARCH seed bank descriptor; Tohono O'odham Community Action

entries.notes: Coastal PNW and Alaska spruce; spring tips harvested for syrup, beer, vinegar. Mild citrus flavor. Largest spruce species; pollinator-friendly tree.
entries.source: University of Alaska Cooperative Extension; USDA Forest Service Pacific Northwest Research Station

entries.notes: Missouri-bred University release with very large cymes, downward-facing (less bird damage). High yield and resilient.
entries.source: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry cultivar descriptor

entries.notes: SW and Texas mesquite. Sweet pods milled into nutty caramel-toned flour, traditional Apache, Comanche, Tohono O'odham staple. Harvest ripe pods in summer, dry, hammer-mill.
entries.source: Native Seeds/SEARCH; San Xavier Co-op Farm seed bank

entries.notes: Mojave clustering barrel cactus. Seeds and fruit eaten by Cahuilla, Mohave. CAUTION: ethical wild harvest only; slow-growing, protected in many areas.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Desert Botanical Garden

entries.notes: SW Sonoran columnar cactus with bristle-tipped tubercles. Small red fruit edible; traditional Comcaac (Seri) food. Frost-tender.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Native Seeds/SEARCH

entries.notes: Mojave keystone yucca; flower buds traditional Cahuilla and Southern Paiute food (roasted). Seeds also edible. CAUTION: protected species, ethical wild harvest only; very slow-growing.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; UC Riverside Botanic Gardens

entries.notes: Larger Pacific lowland subspecies, key Coast Salish food crop. Pit-cook for 24-36 hours to convert inulin to fructose. Plant bulbs in fall.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Burke Museum ethnobotany records

entries.notes: CAUTION: must be cooked thoroughly; raw plant toxic. Young pods, shoots eaten by Cherokee, Iroquois. Primarily medicinal (pleurisy root) and monarch host.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; United Plant Savers

entries.notes: Florida palmetto; ripe black berries acrid but historically eaten by Seminole, Calusa. Primarily medicinal (BPH supplement). Wild harvest regulated in FL.
entries.source: Florida Department of Agriculture; University of Florida IFAS Extension

entries.notes: SE coastal native Lauraceae; aromatic leaves used like bay leaf in Cajun cooking. CAUTION: Laurel Wilt disease decimating populations; consider container culture.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; University of Florida IFAS Extension

entries.notes: SE native; petals edible pickled in vinegar or candied (Japanese-style); flavor ginger-cardamom. Use sparingly. Iconic Southern landscape tree.
entries.source: University of Florida IFAS Extension; Forager Chef Alan Bergo

entries.notes: Feathery serrated leaves, mild peppery mustard flavor. Sow dense on 1/4 inch soil, 4 day blackout, harvest at 2 inches. Yield 8-10 oz per 10x20 tray.
entries.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds microgreens guide; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Purple-veined feathery mustard microgreen. Mild peppery flavor; striking color for salads. Same protocol as green mizuna.
entries.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds microgreens guide; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Mild cabbage flavor, crunchy white-green stems. Fast-germinating; 3 day blackout, harvest at 1.5-2 inches. Yield 10-12 oz per tray.
entries.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds microgreens guide; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Japanese mustard spinach, mild sweet brassica flavor. Tender broad leaves; 3-4 day blackout. Yield 9-11 oz per tray.
entries.source: Kitazawa Seed Company; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: More peppery than standard arugula, slower-growing. Lacy serrated leaves. 4-5 day blackout, harvest at 1.5 inches.
entries.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds microgreens guide; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Smooth broadleaf cress, peppery wasabi-like flavor, milder than curled cress. 2 day blackout, harvest tender at 1.5 inches.
Slow germinator; soak seeds 8 hours first. Feathery fronds, true dill flavor. Harvest at 3-4 inches. Yield modest (5-7 oz per tray).
entries.source: True Leaf Market microgreens guide; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Cinnamon-mint-anise flavor, popular in sushi garnish. Slow germinator (10-14 days). Light required from sowing (light-sensitive germination).
entries.source: Kitazawa Seed Company; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Deep purple-red leaves, complex anise-cinnamon flavor. Same protocol as green shiso. Premium garnish for restaurants.
entries.source: Kitazawa Seed Company; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Edible chrysanthemum microgreen, herbaceous floral flavor. 3-4 day blackout. Used in Japanese nabemono garnish.
entries.source: Kitazawa Seed Company; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Slow grower; succulent lemony stems and leaves. High omega-3. Surface sow, light required for germination, warm soil 75F+.
entries.source: True Leaf Market microgreens guide; Adaptive Seeds catalog

entries.notes: Cucumber-flavored microgreen, fuzzy first true leaves. Soak large seeds 6-8 hours; light cover. Harvest at 2-3 inches.
entries.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Mild clove-cucumber flavor, slim purple-tinged stems. 3-4 day blackout. Specialty restaurant garnish.
Citrus-floral flavor, slim leaves with distinctive marigold aroma. Slow grower; 3 day blackout. Tarragon-like substitute.
Strong licorice-anise flavor, mint family. Surface sow with light pressure; light required for germination. Specialty cocktail garnish.
entries.source: True Leaf Market microgreens guide; Strictly Medicinal Seeds

entries.notes: Lemony mint flavor. Slow to germinate; surface sow, light required. Tiny leaves but intense flavor for tea, cocktail garnish.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Cool minty flavor. Tiny seeds, surface sow, mist regularly. Slow grower; harvest at 1-1.5 inches.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Sweet mild mint flavor. Same protocol as peppermint micro. Slow grower; specialty garnish for desserts and drinks.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Intense thyme flavor in tiny leaves. Surface sow; light required, mist carefully. Slow to harvest size; restaurant specialty.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Sharp oregano flavor, tiny leaves. Slow germinator; surface sow, light required. Mediterranean micro for pizza, pasta finishing.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Sweet milder cousin of oregano. Surface sow, slow grower. Use as finishing herb for chicken, lamb, tomato dishes.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Velvety leaves with full sage flavor at micro stage. Surface sow; light required. Slow germination 10-14 days.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Peppery thyme-like flavor. Surface sow, light required. Used as finishing micro on bean dishes, eggs.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Cucumber-flavored serrated leaves. 3 day blackout, harvest at 2 inches. Refreshing salad addition or fish garnish.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Tart lemony arrow-shaped leaves. 3 day blackout; harvest at 1.5-2 inches. Pair with fish, eggs, salads.
entries.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Narrow strap-leaf Japanese green, mild mustardy flavor. 3 day blackout. Yield 10 oz per 10x20 tray.
entries.source: Kitazawa Seed Company; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Mild lettuce-like flavor, tender pale green leaves. 3 day blackout, harvest at 2 inches. Excellent salad base micro.
entries.source: Kitazawa Seed Company; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Mild sweet Asian green, dark green spoon-shaped leaves. Productive micro; harvest at 2 inches.
Deep purple veined leaves, sharp horseradish-mustard flavor. 3 day blackout. Spicy salad accent.
Large smooth green leaves, hot mustard flavor. Vigorous, productive; 3 day blackout. Yield 12 oz per tray.
entries.source: True Leaf Market; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Striking burgundy-red leaves with green veins, hot wasabi mustard flavor. Excellent restaurant micro for color and bite.
entries.source: True Leaf Market; Kitazawa Seed Company

entries.notes: Extra hot mustard variety bred for wasabi-like heat. Frilly green leaves; sushi and sashimi garnish.
Milder mustard flavor than other B. juncea varieties. Smooth green leaves; gentler kick for everyday salads.
Pinkish-red striking stems, strong fresh onion flavor. Surface sow, 5-7 day blackout under weighted tray for stretching. Harvest with seed cap.
entries.source: True Leaf Market microgreens guide; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Classic onion microgreen, sharp pungent flavor. Same protocol as red onion micro. Harvest at 3-4 inches when seed coats start dropping.
Distinct mild garlic flavor, flat strap leaves. Slow grower, weighted blackout for elongation. Premium Asian-cuisine micro.
entries.source: True Leaf Market microgreens guide; Kitazawa Seed Company

entries.notes: Strong celery flavor in tiny leaves. Slow germination 7-14 days; surface sow, light required. Premium soup and broth garnish.
entries.source: True Leaf Market microgreens guide; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Smooth-leaf disease-resistant spinach. Soak seeds 12 hours, refrigerate 1 day for uniform germination. Harvest at 2-3 inches.
Striking multicolor stems (red, pink, yellow, white). Soak seeds 4-6 hours; 4 day blackout. Yield 10-12 oz per tray.
Deep red stems with green leaves. Same protocol as rainbow chard. Premium color for restaurant plates.
Classic deep red stems and veining. Soak 4-6 hours; 4 day blackout. Sweet earthy flavor.
entries.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds microgreens guide; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Pinkish-striped stems, milder sweet flavor. Italian heritage cultivar at micro stage. Soak seeds first.
entries.source: Adaptive Seeds catalog descriptor; True Leaf Market

entries.notes: Colorful red, pink, yellow stems. Light cover; harvest at 2-3 inches. Nutty earthy flavor, high protein micro.
entries.source: True Leaf Market microgreens guide; Adaptive Seeds

entries.notes: Soak hulled black oil seeds 8-12 hours, weighted blackout 3-4 days to crack hulls. Nutty crunchy shoots; harvest before true leaves emerge.
entries.source: True Leaf Market microgreens guide; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Tendril-rich snow or snap pea selection. Soak 8-12 hours; dense sow. Harvest 4-6 inches; cut-and-come-again twice. Sweet crunchy shoots.
Flat-pod snow pea for shoots; sweeter than snap. Same protocol as tendril pea. Asian dim sum classic; stir-fry or fresh.
entries.source: Kitazawa Seed Company; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Heirloom snow pea with purple bicolor flowers. Productive shoot crop; sweet flavor. Soak 8-12 hours, dense sow.
entries.source: Adaptive Seeds catalog; Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds

entries.notes: Variegated speckled seed coat, traditional dry/soup pea. Vigorous shoot crop. Soak 12 hours; cut-and-come-again.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Adaptive Seeds catalog

entries.notes: Cover-crop pea grown for shoots, often the cheapest bulk pea seed for high-volume shoot production. Sweet productive.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Johnny's Selected Seeds

entries.notes: Soak 8-12 hours, rinse 2x daily. Sprout in jar or tray; harvest when tail is 1/4 to 1 inch (3-5 days). Earthy nutty flavor.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Decorticated red lentils will not sprout; use whole red lentils only. Soak 8 hours; mild flavor, tender texture. 3-day sprout cycle.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Small Spanish brown lentil, nutty rich flavor. Soak 8-12 hours, rinse 2x daily, harvest at 4-6 days.
Soak 4-6 hours, mucilaginous seed coat. Sprout in mesh tray with frequent misting. Hot peppery flavor at 4-7 days.
Sharper hotter mustard than yellow. Soak 4-6 hours, sprout in mesh tray with regular misting. Use in Indian and pickled preparations.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Purple-tinged sprouts with mild kale flavor. Soak 4 hours; rinse 2-3x daily. Crunchy, nutty.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Classic green curly kale variety as sprout. Mild brassica flavor, high in glucoraphanin. Rinse 2-3x daily.
Italian rapini sprout, slightly bitter peppery flavor. Soak 4-6 hours; rinse 2x daily. 5-7 day cycle.
Heirloom Italian broccoli sprout, high sulforaphane precursor (glucoraphanin). Soak 4-6 hours; harvest at 5-6 days.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Mild brassica flavor like broccoli sprout. Soak 4-6 hours; rinse 2x daily. Used for high-sulforaphane supplement-style sprouting.
Pink-rooted radish sprout, fiery hot flavor. Soak 4-6 hours; rinse 2x daily. Pink-tinged stems, white shoots.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Striking purple-red stems with green leaves, peppery radish kick. Premium sprout for visual appeal in salads.
Mild peppery flavor, smooth white-green stems. Soak 4-6 hours; rinse 2x daily. Adult roots are pink-fleshed Asian radish.
Purple-stemmed daikon sprout, sharp mustardy heat. Soak 4-6 hours; rinse 2x daily. Asian salad and banh mi garnish.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Kitazawa Seed Company

entries.notes: Welsh onion (scallion) sprout, slow growing. Soak 4 hours; rinse 2-3x daily. 10-14 day cycle. Strong fresh onion flavor.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Mild sweet leek flavor at sprout stage. Slow growing; soak 4 hours, rinse 2x daily. 10-14 day cycle.
Reddish-tinted clover sprout, mild sweet pea-flavor. Soak 4-6 hours; rinse 2x daily. Often blended with alfalfa.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Sprout People catalog

entries.notes: Tiny seeds, brief sprout cycle (2-3 days). Soak 4 hours; rinse 2x daily. Mild earthy flavor. Pseudo-cereal sprout.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Sprout People catalog

entries.notes: Mucilaginous seed coat (slimy when wet); use mesh tray sprouting not jar. Spritz 3-4x daily. Omega-3 rich; mild nutty.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Sprout People catalog

entries.notes: Same protocol as golden flax; tray sprouting only due to mucilage. Higher lignan content than golden.
Mucilaginous like flax; tray-only sprouting on clay/terracotta or unglazed surface. Mist 4x daily. Mild flavor, omega-3 rich.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Lighter-colored chia variant, same omega-3 content. Tray-sprout only due to mucilage. Mist 4x daily.
Use UNHULLED seeds only (hulled will not sprout). Soak 8 hours; rinse 2x daily; short cycle (2-3 days). Use before bitter taste develops.
Striking black unhulled sesame sprouts, nutty rich flavor. Same protocol as tan sesame. Use quickly before bitterness.
Hull-less Austrian pumpkin seed for sprouting. Soak 6-8 hours; rinse 2x daily. Green-coated nutty sprouts; high zinc.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Sprout People catalog

entries.notes: Use untreated black-seeded watermelon seeds. Soak 8 hours; rinse 2x daily. Mild nutty flavor. Popular in Africa, Middle East.
Use raw unhulled black confection seeds. Soak 8-12 hours; rinse 2-3x daily. Crunchy nutty sprouts at 2-3 days. Distinct from shoot growing.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Sprout People catalog

entries.notes: Korean sprouting soybean variety (kongnamul). Soak 12 hours; rinse 3-4x daily; grow in dark for white tender shoots. COOK before eating (raw soy not edible).
entries.source: Kitazawa Seed Company; Sprout People catalog

entries.notes: Grown longer (4-7 days) for full crunchy sprout vs 2-3 day short sprout. Soak 12 hours; rinse 2-3x daily. Stir-fry favorite.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Kitazawa Seed Company

entries.notes: Mild cabbage flavor at sprout stage. Soak 4-6 hours; rinse 2x daily; harvest at 4-6 days. Use within 1 week.
Mucilaginous seeds; use tray sprouting with paper or terracotta. Peppery flavor; misted 3-4x daily. 5-7 day cycle.
entries.source: Sprout People catalog; Mumm's Sprouting Seeds

entries.notes: Multicolor rainbow blend sprouts; rinse first to remove saponins. Soak 4 hours; very short cycle (2-3 days). Mild nutty.
entries.source: Mumm's Sprouting Seeds; Sprout People catalog

entries.notes: Tropical American indigo, historically grown across Caribbean and Central America. Cut at flower bud for richest dye yield. Tender perennial north of zone 9.
entries.source: Long Thread Media Spin Off feature on indigos; Living Blue grower notes

entries.notes: Highest indican content of cultivated indigos; backbone of African and Indian commercial indigo. Coppice 2-3 times per season once 60 cm tall.
entries.source: Living Blue (Bangladesh) indigo cultivation guide; Maiwa Handprints indigo notes

entries.notes: Cold-hardiest indigo, dies back to root and resprouts. Pink flower spikes ornamental. Lower indican than tropical indigos but viable for cold-climate dyers.
entries.source: Long Thread Media indigo cold-climate guide; USDA NRCS plant introduction notes

entries.notes: Akane yields a brighter orange-red than European madder; root harvest at 3-5 years. Used historically in Japanese kimono dyeing. Prefers light shade.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints natural dye archive; Long Thread Media madder feature

entries.notes: Manjistha is both an Ayurvedic medicinal and a deep crimson dye source. Climbing habit; trellis or let scramble. Roots ready for harvest year 3 onward.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints dye archive; Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India

entries.notes: Cousin to weld with similar luteolin yellow flavonoid; tall white flower spikes. Cut whole plant at full bloom. Self-seeds readily.
entries.source: Long Thread Media weld and Reseda family guide; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Root yields rose-red (madder-family alizarin); flowering tops yield yellow. Spreads aggressively by rhizome; site where it can roam.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints natural dye archive; USDA NRCS plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Cold-climate Galium with similar dye chemistry to Lady's Bedstraw. Boreal native; less aggressive. Harvest roots fall of year 2 or later.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center northern plains notes

entries.notes: Flower heads give clear lemon yellow on wool with alum. Lower yield per area than Dyer's Chamomile but doubles as groundcover and tea herb.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints dye archive; Long Thread Media chamomile dye notes

entries.notes: Recent taxonomic split from Anthemis tinctoria; same butter-yellow dye flowers. Drought tolerant; cut for dye through summer.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints; Long Thread Media dyer's chamomile feature

entries.notes: Tall African marigold mix; 3-4 inch heads in gold and orange. High lutein content for clear yellows on wool. Deadhead for steady dye supply.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints marigold dye notes; Johnny's Selected Seeds catalog descriptor

entries.notes: Pure yellow open-pollinated dye selection; single flowers preferred for easier petal harvest. Use fresh or dry on screens out of sun.
entries.source: Long Thread Media Tagetes dye feature; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Smaller-statured T. patula gives gold to bronze hues. Petal-only dye baths give cleaner color than whole flower. Good companion to fiber beds.
One of the strongest natural dyes available; petals give intense oranges, browns, and pinks depending on pH and mordant. Self-sows reliably.
entries.source: Long Thread Media coreopsis dye feature; USDA NRCS plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Perennial coreopsis with larger flower heads; less concentrated dye than C. tinctoria but easier multi-year harvest. Deadhead aggressively for dye crop.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints; USDA NRCS plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Berries yield fugitive but vivid magenta on wool with vinegar mordant. Toxic to mammals; gloves required for berry harvest. Roots, seeds, leaves all toxic.
entries.source: Long Thread Media pokeberry dye feature; USDA NRCS plant fact sheet (caution toxicity)

entries.notes: Green and black hulls give substantive browns without mordant via juglone tannin. Allelopathic root zone; site away from tomatoes and apples.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints walnut dye archive; USDA NRCS Juglans nigra plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Spotted-petal Mexican dye safflower selected for high carthamin pink. Cold-water extract gives the famous safflower red; warm extract yields yellow.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints safflower dye archive; USDA GRIN safflower descriptors

entries.notes: Spanish dye-line safflower, deep red-orange florets; spineless leaf form prized for hand harvest. Soil moisture during bud stage drives flower count.
entries.source: USDA GRIN safflower germplasm descriptor; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Three crimson stigmas per autumn flower yield culinary spice and a brilliant gold dye on silk. Plant corms August in well-drained sandy soil.
entries.source: USDA Cooperative Extension saffron production guide; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Tropical shrub yielding bixin-rich red seeds for both food coloring and natural dye. North of zone 10 grow as greenhouse tub plant.
entries.source: USDA tropical crop fact sheet; Maiwa Handprints annatto dye archive

entries.notes: Bright yellow berberine-rich inner bark and roots give a clear yellow. Berries also dye but are fugitive. Harvest sparingly; slow-growing native.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints; USDA NRCS Pacific Northwest plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Inner bark, root, and stem give golden yellow via berberine. Note: alternate host of wheat stem rust; banned in some US wheat-growing counties.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints; USDA APHIS regulated plant notice

entries.notes: Tannin-rich Southwest dock; roots yield warm browns and golds. Drought tolerant; goes dormant in summer heat. Tuberous root harvest year 2 onward.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Tucson Plant Materials Center notes; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Hot-color cosmos gives oranges, peaches, and rusts on wool and silk. Diascorin-rich petals; harvest fully open flowers. Self-sows where summer is warm.
entries.source: Long Thread Media cosmos dye feature; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Compact Thai selection; deep crimson calyces for tea and pink-to-purple dye baths. Short-day flowering; plan accordingly above zone 8.
entries.source: Baker Creek (Rare Seeds) catalog descriptor; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Dutch trade selection; larger calyces than Thai Red, milder flavor. Use fresh calyces for cleanest dye color; dried calyces give browner reds.
entries.source: Baker Creek catalog descriptor; Adaptive Seeds notes

entries.notes: Mediterranean borage relative; alkannin-rich root gives crimson on oil and wax (lip balms, leather). Slow from seed; sow fresh in fall.
entries.source: Strictly Medicinal Seeds catalog descriptor; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Source of shikonin; roots give Japanese murasaki purple. Three-year root crop. Tricky from seed; cold-stratify 8 weeks.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints murasaki feature; Japan Society of Dye Plants reference

entries.notes: Flowering tops give yellow to red depending on mordant and pH; hypericin yields red oil extracts. Listed noxious in some western states.
entries.source: Maiwa Handprints; Strictly Medicinal Seeds catalog notes

entries.notes: Plume tassels give greenish-yellow dye. Invasive non-native lineage dominates eastern US wetlands; verify native subspecies before planting.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Phragmites identification guide; Maiwa Handprints

entries.notes: Dutch tall-stem fiber flax; long, fine line fiber for hand spinners. Sow dense (2000 seeds per sq meter) for unbranched stems. Pull at lower-leaf yellowing.
entries.source: Fibershed flax-to-linen guide; Long Thread Media Andrea cultivar feature

entries.notes: Estonian heirloom from the port of Pernau (Parnu). Cold-tolerant; reliable in short northern seasons. Medium-length fiber.
entries.source: Long Thread Media European flax cultivar guide; USDA GRIN flax accession notes

entries.notes: Northern Irish Stormont breeding line; high fiber yield, blue flower. Bred for damp maritime climates. Dew-ret in field 14-21 days.
entries.source: AFBI Northern Ireland flax variety notes; Fibershed

entries.notes: Czech fiber flax with good lodging resistance. Workhorse cultivar for hand processors learning the crop. Pale-blue flowers.
entries.source: European Flax Linen Council cultivar register; Fibershed

entries.notes: French Picardy fiber selection; very fine line fiber suitable for damask weaves. Demands rich loam and consistent moisture.
entries.source: European Flax Linen Council; Long Thread Media

entries.notes: San Joaquin Valley Acala upland; long staple (1.15 in), strong fiber for fine yarns. Open-bolled at maturity. Needs 200+ frost-free days.
entries.source: USDA Cotton Breeding Program (Shafter, CA) descriptor; Fibershed cotton guide

entries.notes: Mid-South upland workhorse; smooth-leaf, stormproof bolls. Conventional (non-GE) seed sometimes available; ask supplier directly.
entries.source: USDA Cotton Variety Trial reports (Mississippi, Texas); Fibershed

entries.notes: Deltapine mid-maturity upland; reliable yields across Cotton Belt. Strong fiber with good micronaire for mill spinning.
entries.source: USDA Cotton Variety Trial reports; Mississippi State Extension

entries.notes: Storm-resistant boll, full-season upland. Common in Carolina-Georgia. Pick at first dry day after 65% boll open.
entries.source: USDA Cotton Variety Trial reports; Georgia Cooperative Extension

entries.notes: USDA Sea Island lineage; 1.5 inch extra-long staple. Late season, heat-demanding. Hand pick to preserve fiber length.
entries.source: USDA Pima Cotton Breeding Program (Maricopa, AZ); Fibershed

entries.notes: Naturally pigmented brown extra-long staple; cherished Gullah-Geechee heirloom. Cool storage prevents fiber color drift.
entries.source: Sally Fox naturally colored cotton archive; Fibershed heirloom cotton notes

entries.notes: California Pima selection bred for hot dry valleys. Drip irrigation friendly; defoliate naturally with cool nights pre-harvest.
entries.source: USDA Pima Cotton Breeding Program; Sun Belt Extension

entries.notes: Historic Egyptian extra-long staple, foundation of fine sheet trade. Long season; lodges in wind, stake or windbreak in exposed plots.
entries.source: Egyptian Cotton Association archive; USDA GRIN G. barbadense descriptors

entries.notes: Indian native cotton; short staple, drought tolerant, perennial in zones 10+. Roots and stems persist; used in handloom khadi traditions.
entries.source: USDA GRIN G. arboreum descriptors; Indian Council of Agricultural Research

entries.notes: Old World A-genome cotton from Arabia and East Africa. Short coarse fiber but exceptional heat-drought tolerance. Bushy 1-2 m plants.
entries.source: USDA GRIN G. herbaceum descriptors; Fibershed heirloom cotton archive

entries.notes: Wild Mexican G. hirsutum relative; small bolls in cream and tan. Sacred to Oaxacan handweavers (coyuche). Slow growing; coppice for fresh fiber.
entries.source: USDA GRIN G. hirsutum wild relative descriptors; Centro de Investigaciones Oaxaca textile archive

entries.notes: Endemic Hawaiian cotton (mao); short brown lint, salt and drought tolerant. Conservation status varies by island; grow from cultivated stock only.
entries.source: Bishop Museum endemic flora notes; USDA GRIN G. tomentosum descriptor

entries.notes: Tenacissima form; silver underside of leaves. 2-3 cuts per year in warm climates. Fiber needs degumming with lye to remove pectin.
entries.source: USDA tropical fiber crop guide; Long Thread Media ramie feature

entries.notes: Nipononivea form; uniformly green leaves, slightly cold-hardier than white ramie. Cut stems just before bloom for finest fiber.
entries.source: Japan Fiber Plant Research Center notes; Long Thread Media

entries.notes: Taiwanese photoperiod-sensitive kenaf; tall stems for bast fiber and paper pulp. Late flowering pushes biomass; harvest at first flower for fiber quality.
USDA-released cultivar (1980s) for southern US kenaf trials. Smooth stems, low spine; easier hand harvest than spiny lines.
entries.source: USDA Whitten kenaf release notes; Mississippi State Extension

entries.notes: Florida-bred kenaf, root-knot nematode tolerant. Tall (4 m) under long warm season; reduce planting density for fiber over biomass.
Caribbean accession with deep root, drought tolerance. Slightly earlier flowering than Tainung 2. Cut and field-ret 2-4 weeks.
Bangladeshi monsoon crop; round seedpods, white fiber. Water-ret bundles for 10-21 days in standing water. Tolerates wet feet.
Long-podded tossa jute; finer, stronger fiber than capsularis. Leaves edible as ewedu/molokhia. Dual-purpose food and fiber crop.
entries.source: Bangladesh Jute Research Institute; ECHO Community tropical agriculture notes

entries.notes: Indian Jute Research selection (Navin); high fiber yield, premature flowering resistance. Sow Mar-Apr in northern India equivalent latitudes.
entries.source: Indian Central Research Institute for Jute and Allied Fibres (CRIJAF) descriptor

entries.notes: Improved CRIJAF Sufala selection; fine luster bast, good for blended yarn. Cut at small-pod stage for fiber finer than late-cut.
Yucatecan twine agave; shorter, coarser fiber than sisal but more cold-tolerant. Cut lower leaves at 5-7 years and on through plant lifespan.
entries.source: Yucatan Henequen Heritage program archive; USDA tropical fiber notes

entries.notes: Chihuahuan Desert agave relative; long stiff fiber leaves. Drought-hardy clump-former. Researched as bast pulp source.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Tucson Plant Materials Center fact sheet

entries.notes: Andean fique fiber agave; backbone of Colombian and Ecuadorian rope. Monocarpic; harvest leaves over decades before flowering.
entries.source: Colombian Cabuya Heritage archive; USDA tropical fiber crop notes

entries.notes: Caribbean rope agave, naturalized across tropics. Stiff white fiber for cordage. Aggressive; can escape cultivation in zones 10+.
Compact bronze cultivar of harakeke. Ornamental plus traditional Maori fiber use (muka). Harvest outer leaves leaving central rito.
entries.source: Royal Horticultural Society Phormium descriptor; Te Roopu Raranga Whatu Aotearoa harakeke guide

entries.notes: Drooping yellow-and-green striped foliage. Ornamental priority; fiber softer than green forms. Mulch crown in zone 8 winters.
Pink-margined olive leaves; ornamental focal point. Slower to clump than green types. Fiber suitable for coarse cordage.
Rose-bronze striping on green; named for Maori weaving heritage. Vigorous; clumps to 1.5 m. Outer leaves split easily for ribbon weaving.
entries.source: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network; RHS Phormium register

entries.notes: Apricot-pink leaf striping with bronze margins. Mid-size; 1.2 m tall. Fiber best from mature 2 year old leaves.
entries.source: RHS Phormium register; NZ Plant Conservation Network

entries.notes: Bronze-green leaves with rose pink margins; tall (2 m). Strong vertical accent. Reliable performer for coastal sites with salt spray.
NZ ti kouka; long sword leaves give strong Maori cordage fiber. Slow to fiber-quality maturity (5+ years). Trunk-forming tree habit.
entries.source: Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research NZ plant database

entries.notes: Madagascar screwpine; long spiny leaves for Pacific hat and mat weaving. Strip thorns before splitting. Salt-tolerant coastal species.
entries.source: USDA tropical fiber crop guide; Pacific Island Agroforestry

entries.notes: Hala in Hawaii, lauhala fiber tradition. Aerial prop roots; tolerates salt and wind. Fruit segments also edible after long roasting.
entries.source: Bishop Museum hala fiber archive; USDA tropical agriculture

entries.notes: Philippine fiber banana; leaf sheaths strip-decorticated to long pale fibers. World's strongest natural cellulose fiber. Needs 80+ inches rain.
entries.source: Philippine Fiber Industry Development Authority guide

entries.notes: Plains soapweed; narrow leaves give the cordage fiber used by Plains nations for ropes and sandals. Roots also yield saponin soap.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Plains Plant Materials Center notes

entries.notes: Trunk-forming coastal yucca with sharp tipped leaves. Stiff fiber for brushes and rough cordage. Gloves and eye protection during harvest.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Florida plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Eastern Adam's Needle, fibrous leaf margins curl off as ready-made thread. Cherokee and Catawba fiber tradition. Hardy to zone 4.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center southeastern fact sheet

entries.notes: Traditional bast fiber across North America for cordage and nets. Toxic milky sap; cattle avoid. Harvest dry winter stems for fiber, never green.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Buckskin Revolution fiber archive

entries.notes: Seedpod silk floss historically used as life-jacket fill. Stem bast also makes coarse fiber. Plant for monarchs first; harvest as secondary use.
entries.source: Xerces Society milkweed guide; USDA NRCS plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Wet-site milkweed; finer bast fiber than common milkweed. Eastern fiber tradition for thread and netting. Pollinator priority crop.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; Xerces Society

entries.notes: European bast fiber tradition; cut at flowering for finest fiber. Dew-ret 2-3 weeks. Distinct from medicinal stinging-nettle entry; same plant, fiber use.
entries.source: Stinging Nettle Network UK guide; Long Thread Media nettle fiber feature

entries.notes: Perennial fiber flax with weaker fiber than L. usitatissimum but multi-year crop. Lewis flax type; sky blue flowers. Drought tolerant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center; Long Thread Media

entries.notes: Rare mid-Atlantic native; bast fiber and biomass energy candidate. 3 m stems; coppice annually for fiber. Endangered in wild; cultivate from nursery stock.
entries.source: USDA NRCS rare plant fact sheet; Polish energy crop research

entries.notes: Pantropical coastal tree (hau in Hawaii); inner bark gives strong cordage. Salt-tolerant; common in Polynesian fiber traditions.
Arid-zone shrub; seed floss called akund used as kapok substitute. Toxic latex; avoid contact with skin and eyes. Can become invasive in dry climates.
entries.source: USDA tropical fiber crop guide; Indian Council of Agricultural Research arid crop notes

entries.notes: Caribbean terrestrial bromeliad; spiny leaves yield strong silvery fiber. Traditional Mesoamerican hedge plus fiber crop. Edible fruit by-product.
entries.source: USDA tropical fiber crop archive; Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute

entries.notes: Pita fiber; coarser than sisal but cold-hardier (zone 8). Cut lower leaves at 5+ years. Monocarpic; produces fiber until final flowering.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Tucson Plant Materials Center fact sheet

entries.notes: Indian Sun Hemp dual-use: cover crop nitrogen plus bast fiber for paper and rope. Cut at flowering for fiber; before pod set is critical.
entries.source: USDA NRCS sunn hemp guide; Indian Council of Agricultural Research

entries.notes: Vine bast fiber for Japanese kuzu cloth. CAUTION: federally listed noxious in much of US; do not plant where not already established. Harvest only.
entries.source: USDA APHIS noxious weed list; Japan Kuzu Textile Heritage notes

entries.notes: Inner bark of vines yields fujifu cloth fiber in Japanese tradition. Harvest from prunings of established vines; trellis for management.
entries.source: Japan Textile Heritage Center fujifu archive

entries.notes: Bast fiber of tapa cloth (Pacific) and washi paper (Japan). Coppice 1-year shoots in winter. Aggressive root suckering; site with care.
entries.source: Hawaiian Tapa Heritage archive; Japan washi-making guide

entries.notes: Arctic bog sedge; seed bristles historically used as wick and pillow stuffing in Scandinavia and Inuit traditions. Requires acid wet soils.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Alaska plant fact sheet; Nordic Fiber Plant Network notes

entries.notes: Inner bark fiber for cordage, baskets, mats; Indigenous Great Lakes tradition (Ojibwe wiigob). Coppice young trees rather than stripping mature trunks.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Tilia americana fact sheet; Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission ethnobotany notes

entries.notes: Egyptian papyrus sedge; stem pith laminated to make papyrus sheets. Aquatic; grow in 6-12 inches standing water. Hardy to zone 9 with mulched roots.
entries.source: Egyptian Papyrus Institute archive; USDA aquatic plant guide

entries.notes: USDA NRCS purple osier release for streambank stabilization and basketry. Long flexible rods; coppice annually in dormancy. Plant cuttings 12 in deep.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Big Flats Plant Materials Center release notes

entries.notes: NRCS purple osier selection from Pennsylvania. Fine-stemmed; preferred for tight basketwork. Tolerates wet feet.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Big Flats Plant Materials Center release notes

entries.notes: European basketmaker purple; deep mahogany rods. Strip in spring as bark loosens for green or peeled white work.
Vigorous common osier hybrid; long straight rods to 2.5 m in one season. Workhorse for larger baskets and hurdles.
French Brittany osier; mid-green rods. Reliable annual coppice. Strong base material that pairs with finer-stem cultivars for accents.
Almond willow; rod splits beautifully for fine skeined work. Black Maul subtype prized by chair-bottom seat weavers.
Stems for thatch, basketry, mats. Distinguish native subspecies americanus from invasive europaeus before introducing to new wetlands.
Tule of western Native American mat traditions. Aquatic; grow in 4-12 in standing water. Cut stems in late summer for mat weaving.
entries.source: USDA NRCS plant fact sheet; California Indian Basketweavers Association

entries.notes: Tall arching sedge; long leaves used in European basketry and chair seats. Shade tolerant. Cut second-year growth in late summer.
entries.source: RHS Carex profile; UK Basketmakers Association notes

entries.notes: Fen sedge used in Indigenous Great Lakes basketry. Limey wet soils. Cut in late summer when leaves fully extended.
entries.source: USDA NRCS native sedge fact sheet; Great Lakes ethnobotany resources

entries.notes: Soft rush stems split and braided for tatami edging, mats, and chair seats. Wet soil staple. Coppice clumps annually.
entries.source: USDA NRCS wetland plant fact sheet; Japan Igusa tatami archive

entries.notes: Sacred to many North American First Nations for braiding. Cultivate from divisions, never wild-collect; commercial wild harvest threatens native stands.
entries.source: United Plant Savers at-risk species notes; Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission

entries.notes: Vines used widely in Appalachian basketry; harvest from established invasive stands rather than planting new. Boil and peel bark for cream-colored weavers.
entries.source: USDA Forest Service Japanese honeysuckle management note; Appalachian basketmaker tradition

entries.notes: Riverbank grape vines for rustic basketry and wreaths. Cut dormant 1-2 year canes. Soak in water 24 hours before bending.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Vitis riparia plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Silica-rich stems used as natural sandpaper and in fine basket embellishment. Aggressive; site contained in pots or barriers.
Canadian late-heading timothy; widely grown for hay. Higher yields than Alta but later cutting date. Cut at boot stage for horse-quality hay.
entries.source: Saskatchewan Forage Variety guide; Oregon State Forage Information System

entries.notes: Northern Plains release with strong winter survival and tiller density. Pairs well with red clover. Cut at first head emergence.
entries.source: NDSU Forage Variety Trials; Saskatchewan Forage guide

entries.notes: Late-maturing AAFC release; aphid-tolerant. Reliable second cut. Good fit for stands kept 4+ years.
entries.source: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada cultivar release notes

entries.notes: European late-heading type; broad leaves, high palatability. Common in horse hay blends across the Northeast.
entries.source: Pennsylvania State Extension forage variety notes

entries.notes: Mid-late maturity; AAFC release favored in eastern Canada. Strong tiller density. Avoid grazing first year.
Early-medium maturity; useful for harmonizing harvest with alfalfa mixes. Persistent on heavier soils.
Russian-developed cold-tolerant timothy. Strong overwintering in northern plains. Mid-late heading.
entries.source: Saskatchewan Forage guide; AAFC cultivar register

entries.notes: Norwegian winter-hardy selection; medium maturity, fine leaves. Suits sheep and goat pasture.
Late-maturing Scandinavian type; preferred for late hay cuts in cool wet summers. Good aftermath regrowth.
Medium-late maturity; high digestibility for dairy and horse hay. Pairs with red clover in 3-cut systems.
Released for stand longevity under intensive cutting. Resists summer slump in transition-zone pastures.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center release notes

entries.notes: New Zealand late-heading orchardgrass; matches with white clover in dairy pastures. Slow autumn growth.
European late-heading line; reliable second cut. Suits 4-cut intensive grazing rotations.
Cold-tolerant Eastern European orchardgrass; rust resistant. Strong spring vigor. Common in Wisconsin-Minnesota trials.
entries.source: UW Madison Forage Trials; European Plant Variety Database

entries.notes: DLF Pickseed late-heading line; fine leaves, high RFQ. Mixes well with alfalfa for hay.
entries.source: DLF Pickseed cultivar register; Oregon State Forage Information System

entries.notes: Mid-maturity, leaf rust tolerant. Adaptable across the Northeast. Pair with alfalfa in 3-cut systems.
entries.source: Penn State Extension forage variety notes

entries.notes: USDA Pullman release; late-maturing, drought tolerant. Long-stand orchardgrass for Western pastures.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Pullman Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Nebraska release (1942); southern smooth brome adapted to Plains states. Good hay grass with alfalfa.
Northern Canadian release; winter-hardy to zone 2. Slow to spread by rhizome but persistent. Cut at heading.
New York release; intermediate smooth brome with broad adaptation. Reliable across the Northeast and Midwest.
USDA Pullman release from Manchurian seed source. Drought tolerant; preferred for inland Pacific Northwest.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Pullman Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Canadian release for the prairies; high leaf-to-stem ratio. Mixes with alfalfa.
Improved aftermath regrowth; suited for 2 to 3 cut hay systems on the Plains. Vigorous spring growth.
AAFC release; bunchgrass habit (less aggressive than smooth brome). Better regrowth than smooth brome under rotational grazing.
entries.source: AAFC cultivar register; Saskatchewan Forage Variety Guide

entries.notes: USDA Aberdeen release for Intermountain West. Drought tolerant; high palatability. Pair with alfalfa.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Aberdeen Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: AAFC selection with strong fall regrowth. Earlier maturity than Paddock. Reliable in mixed Canadian forage stands.
USDA Aberdeen 1966 release; drought tolerant, high palatability. Long-time standard for Mountain West.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Aberdeen Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Short-lived perennial native bunchgrass; quick establishment for reclamation. Bridge cover until longer-lived species take over.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center fact sheet

entries.notes: Endophyte-free continental tall fescue; safer for horses. Lower persistence than endophyte-infected types in heat-stressed regions.
entries.source: Penn State Extension forage variety guide

entries.notes: European continental type; soft leaves, high palatability. Endophyte-free. Best on cool moist sites.
entries.source: DLF Pickseed cultivar register; Oregon State Forage Information System

entries.notes: Soft-leaf endophyte-friendly continental type for grazing. Improved cool-season production.
Novel non-toxic endophyte (AR542); avoids fescue toxicosis while keeping persistence. Major improvement over wild-type KY-31.
entries.source: University of Georgia Forage Extension MaxQ trials

entries.notes: Southern adapted non-toxic novel endophyte tall fescue. Heat and drought tolerant for transition-zone South.
entries.source: Noble Research Institute Texoma MaxQ II release notes

entries.notes: Selected for elevated magnesium; reduces grass tetany risk in early spring grazing. Softer leaf than tall fescue.
entries.source: University of Wisconsin Forage Variety Trials

entries.notes: USDA Wisconsin release tracing to historic 1880s Driftless Area pasture stands. Long-lived; high palatability.
entries.source: USDA Dairy Forage Research Center release notes

entries.notes: Fine bunch fescue; low-input pasture filler for poor soils. Slow to establish but persistent. Good for sheep.
Canadian release; cold-tolerant creeping red fescue for marginal northern pastures. Tolerates shade and acidic soils.
Penn State release; shade tolerant. Low-maintenance pasture and lawn-pasture overlap species.
entries.source: Penn State Extension turf and forage notes

entries.notes: Oregon State release; early Willamette Valley perennial ryegrass. Short-lived but vigorous; common in pasture mixes.
entries.source: Oregon State University Forage Information System

entries.notes: Dutch winter-hardy perennial ryegrass. Improved persistence for cool-temperate pastures.
Rutgers University release; fine-leaved turf-type ryegrass adapted to dual pasture-lawn use.
entries.source: Rutgers University Plant Breeding release notes

entries.notes: Penn State release; medium-leaf perennial ryegrass for transition-zone pastures. Strong stand density.
Dual purpose pasture-turf release; quick germination, dense tiller habit. Good for over-seeding.
entries.source: Oregon State Forage Information System; turfgrass trial reports

entries.notes: Mississippi release; cold-tolerant annual ryegrass for southeastern winter pasture. Strong fall and early spring growth.
entries.source: Mississippi State Extension annual ryegrass guide

entries.notes: Tetraploid annual ryegrass; higher sugars and palatability. Spring stockpile crop.
Southern annual ryegrass standard; common in Florida-Texas winter overseed of dormant bermudagrass.
entries.source: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension winter pasture guide

entries.notes: Late-maturing southern annual ryegrass; extends Gulf Coast grazing season into late spring.
entries.source: University of Florida Cooperative Extension forage guide

entries.notes: French tetraploid Italian ryegrass; cold tolerant, late-maturing. Suits northern winter cover and grazing.
Tetraploid annual ryegrass; broader leaves, higher palatability than diploid types. Common in cover crop mixes.
Welsh Aberystwyth hybrid; combines Italian vigor with perennial persistence. 3-4 year stand life.
entries.source: IBERS Aberystwyth University Lolium breeding notes

entries.notes: Tetraploid hybrid (perenne x multiflorum). High dry matter yield first 18 months. Pair with red clover.
Low-alkaloid reed canarygrass for wet sites and stream buffers. Avoid letting it head out (avoids palatability drop and seed escape).
entries.source: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Low-alkaloid Canadian release with high palatability. Useful for buffering manure runoff while making hay.
Improved low-alkaloid release; persistent on wet soils. Pre-cut at boot stage before heading.
Pasture-type Kentucky bluegrass; less tightly sodded than turf types. Productive on droughty hill pastures.
entries.source: Penn State Extension forage variety guide

entries.notes: Minnesota release; quick establishment under cool spring conditions. Used in Plains pasture renovation.
USDA hybrid (A. cristatum x A. desertorum); broad western range adaptation. Early spring forage on dry sites.
entries.source: USDA ARS Forage and Range Research Lab release

entries.notes: Canadian release for saline soils; hybrid of crested and quackgrass. Reclaim salt-affected pastures with this species.
entries.source: AAFC Swift Current Research Centre cultivar release

entries.notes: USDA Mandan release; broad-leaf crested wheatgrass for the Plains. Cold-hardy to zone 2. Spring grazing standard.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bismarck Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Fine-leaved Canadian crested wheatgrass; persistent under heavy grazing. Common in CRP and reclamation seed mixes.
USDA Bridger PMC release of native slender wheatgrass. Quick-establishing reclamation species; saline tolerant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: UNL release; broad-leaf intermediate wheatgrass with high palatability. Strong second-cut potential.
AAFC Lethbridge release; drought tolerant Prairie type. Good fit for late-season pasture extension.
Pubescent (hairy-leaf) intermediate wheatgrass; drought tolerant subspecies. AAFC release for arid Plains pastures.
USDA Pullman release; salt-tolerant tall wheatgrass for reclaiming sodic and saline pastures. Tall coarse forage.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Pullman Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: New Mexico tall wheatgrass release; deep rooted, salt tolerant. Useful for windbreak strips and salty pasture corners.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Montana native western wheatgrass release. Strongly rhizomatous; soil holding species for the northern Plains.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Colorado native western wheatgrass release. Drought tolerant; spring cool-season forage on short-grass prairie.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Meeker Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Foundation Intermountain native bunchgrass; not tolerant of close grazing. Deferred grazing through boot stage protects stands.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Aberdeen Plant Materials Center notes

entries.notes: Awnless form of bluebunch wheatgrass; preferred for horse pastures. Conservation grazing standard.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center notes

entries.notes: Sweet-stem sudangrass for summer grazing. Wait until plant is 24 in tall before grazing to avoid prussic acid risk.
entries.source: Penn State Extension summer annual forage guide

entries.notes: Fine-stem sudangrass hybrid; high regrowth. Cut or graze at 30 in for best feed quality and prussic acid safety.
entries.source: Pennington Seed cultivar register; UNL forage guide

entries.notes: Hairs-type leaf sudangrass; reduced prussic acid risk relative to early hybrids. Drought tolerant summer pasture.
entries.source: Texas A&M AgriLife summer forage guide

entries.notes: Sweet brown-mid-rib sorghum-sudangrass with high palatability. Multi-cut summer forage; pair with cowpea for protein.
entries.source: Penn State Extension summer annual forage guide

entries.notes: Brown-midrib gene reduces lignin; significantly improved digestibility. Common in dairy summer haylage rations.
entries.source: USDA ARS forage sorghum BMR research notes

entries.notes: Quick-establishing hybrid; 60-90 day grazing window. Standard for emergency summer hay after wheat or winter forage.
entries.source: Texas A&M AgriLife summer forage variety guide

entries.notes: BMR sorghum-sudan hybrid with sweet sap; high palatability for dairy. Plant after soil reaches 65 F.
Tifton release; leafy dwarf pearl millet for grazing. No prussic acid risk (unlike sorghum-sudan). Tolerates sandy acid soils.
entries.source: USDA ARS Tifton, Georgia release notes

entries.notes: Tall sugar-stem pearl millet for silage and grazing. High dry matter yield in hot dry summers.
entries.source: University of Georgia Extension pearl millet guide

entries.notes: Hybrid pearl millet for forage; rapid summer growth and multiple cuts. Replant after wheat or winter pea.
Oklahoma forage crabgrass release; useful summer pasture in transition-zone South. Reseeds aggressively year on year.
entries.source: Noble Research Institute Red River crabgrass release notes

entries.notes: Quick establishing, large-leaf forage crabgrass. Pairs with bermudagrass to fill mid-summer slumps.
entries.source: Noble Research Institute Quick-N-Big release notes

entries.notes: USDA Manhattan Kansas release; native warm-season gamagrass. Slow to establish but extremely persistent. Cut twice per season.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Manhattan Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Mississippi gamagrass release; adapted to southeastern bottomland soils. Cold stratify seed before spring sowing.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Coffeeville Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: New Mexico release; drought tolerant mid-grass native. State grass of Texas. Slow to establish.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Oklahoma release; broad central Plains adaptation. Sideoats grama state-of-Texas heritage species.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Manhattan Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: New Mexico southern Plains release; drought tolerant. Plant on well-drained soils for best stand longevity.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: New Mexico blue grama release; drought tolerant. Short-grass prairie staple. Slow to establish; weed control critical year 1.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: South Dakota native blue grama ecotype; cold-hardy short-grass prairie restoration. Pair with sideoats and buffalograss for native pasture.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bismarck Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Northern Plains blue grama release; cold-hardy. Foundation species for mixed-grass prairie restoration in Montana and Dakotas.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Texas-Oklahoma buffalograss release; sod-forming short-grass prairie native. Low water; minimal mowing for low-input pasture or lawn.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Knox City Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Texas release; deeper green than Texoka. Drought and heat tolerant. Common in Plains pasture and rangeland reseeding.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Knox City Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Nebraska short-grass prairie buffalograss release. Sod-forming; tolerates heavy grazing once established.
Southwestern short-grass; survives extreme drought. Stoloniferous; forms low mats. Valuable for arid rangeland renovation.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Tucson Plant Materials Center plant fact sheet

entries.notes: Fall dormancy 4, winter survival 2. Salt tolerant; suited for irrigated Southwest and Great Plains hay rotations.
entries.source: Forage Genetics International WL alfalfa cultivar register

entries.notes: Fall dormancy 5 high-traffic-tolerant alfalfa; broad disease resistance. Strong fit for southern Plains 4-cut systems.
entries.source: Forage Genetics International WL alfalfa cultivar register

entries.notes: Upper Midwest forage alfalfa; FD 3, winter hardy. Bacterial wilt and Phytophthora resistant.
Northern verticillium-resistant alfalfa. FD 2. Winter-hardy hybrid for cold-winter dairy regions.
Kashmir-derived dryland alfalfa; FD 3. Cold and drought hardy. Long-stand variety for marginal northern pastures.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Nebraska 1942 release; historic winter-hardy bacterial wilt resistant alfalfa. Still grown for legacy hay-meadow stands.
Creeping-rooted (M. falcata heritage) alfalfa; persistent under grazing. Good fit for irrigated pasture.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: FD 4 traffic-tolerant alfalfa; suited for dairy fields under heavy equipment. Strong disease resistance.
entries.source: America's Alfalfa cultivar register; UW Madison Forage Trials

entries.notes: FD 4 with reduced-lignin trait for delayed maturity and higher RFQ. Allows wider cutting window without quality loss.
Italian Po Valley origin; FD 5-6. Heat tolerant; useful in Mediterranean climates and irrigated California pastures.
New York release; bacterial wilt resistant. Reliable for Adirondack and New England hay meadows.
AAFC yellow-flowered alfalfa release. Extreme drought and cold tolerance; grazing-tolerant rangeland alfalfa.
entries.source: AAFC Saskatoon Research Centre cultivar release

entries.notes: USDA Nebraska release; biennial yellow sweet clover with good first-year forage yield. Annual fields with this for fast nectar and forage.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Manhattan Plant Materials Center notes

entries.notes: Iowa State annual white sweetclover; first-year flowering and seed set. Quick green manure and bee forage rotation.
entries.source: Iowa State Extension sweet clover guide

entries.notes: Low-coumarin biennial white sweetclover; reduces dicumarol risk in cured hay. AAFC release.
entries.source: AAFC cultivar register; Saskatchewan Forage Variety Guide

entries.notes: Low-coumarin yellow sweetclover release; bee pasture standard. Cuts must dry fast to avoid dicumarol formation.
Wisconsin release; long-lived red clover (3+ years). Powdery mildew tolerant. Pair with timothy for hay.
Kentucky 1947 release; medium red clover, anthracnose resistant. Long the standard southern medium clover.
entries.source: University of Kentucky Extension forage guide

entries.notes: Improved long-lived medium red clover; high seedling vigor. Better persistence than older Kenland-type clovers.
entries.source: Pickseed cultivar register; UW Forage Trials

entries.notes: Tetraploid medium red clover; high yield and vigor. Use in 3 to 4 year hay rotations.
Low-pubescence red clover; reduced slobbers risk in horses (lower fungal endophyte load on hairs). 2-3 year stand.
entries.source: University of Wisconsin Forage Trials; Penn State Extension

entries.notes: Tetraploid medium red clover; high RFQ for dairy hay. Strong second-year regrowth.
Welsh IBERS tetraploid red clover; persistent under cutting and grazing. Larger leaves than diploid types.
entries.source: IBERS Aberystwyth University Trifolium breeding notes

entries.notes: Intermediate-leaf grazing white clover. Persistent on hill pastures. Pair with perennial ryegrass.
Large-leaf irrigated-pasture white clover; California Imperial Valley standard. High protein. Not winter-hardy north of zone 5.
entries.source: University of California Cooperative Extension forage guide

entries.notes: Pennsylvania large-leaf white clover; cold tolerant Ladino-type. Workhorse for Northeast pasture stands.
entries.source: Penn State Extension Pilgrim release notes

entries.notes: Large-leaf Ladino-type white clover; high yield. Common in dairy pasture seedings.
Northern cold-hardy white clover (Belgian release). Small-medium leaf, high stolon density. Survives zone 3 winters.
IBERS small-leaf white clover; persistent under sheep grazing. High stolon density.
entries.source: IBERS Aberystwyth University Trifolium breeding notes

entries.notes: Multicut Egyptian clover; 3-5 cuts per season. High protein. Frost-sensitive south of zone 8 only.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Beltsville berseem release notes

entries.notes: Stoloniferous clover for wet alkaline soils. Salt tolerant. Pink calyces become inflated like small strawberries at seed set.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Lockeford Plant Materials Center fact sheet

entries.notes: Quick-establishing annual Persian clover; high winter forage on heavy soils. Tolerates wet feet better than crimson.
entries.source: Texas A&M AgriLife winter forage variety guide

entries.notes: Australian Persian clover release; flood tolerant. Heavy reseeding annual; useful in subterranean clover rotations.
Mid-season Australian sub clover; persistent through Mediterranean-climate summer dormancy. Pacific Northwest winter pasture.
entries.source: Oregon State University Cooperative Extension subterranean clover guide

entries.notes: Late-maturing Australian sub clover; suited to longer wet seasons. Strong reseeder. Tolerates moderately acid soils.
Auburn improved arrowleaf clover; late-maturing winter annual. Adapted to upper South pastures. Reseeds reliably.
Reseeding winter annual clover for southern transition zone. Small white flower balls; useful on heavy clay soils.
entries.source: Mississippi State Extension small clover guide

entries.notes: California Mediterranean reseeding annual; drought tolerant. Used on shallow soils where sub clover fails.
entries.source: University of California Cooperative Extension rose clover guide

entries.notes: Small yellow-flowered annual clover; nitrogen fixing groundcover. Self-seeding for rough pastures.
Auburn low-tannin sericea selection; reduced bitterness for better palatability. Note: listed invasive in Kansas and Colorado.
entries.source: Auburn University Extension sericea guide; Kansas Department of Agriculture noxious species list

entries.notes: Auburn low-tannin sericea; selected for higher digestibility. Check state invasive status before planting.
USDA NRCS reclamation sericea; tolerates acid mine soils. CAUTION: listed noxious in multiple states; restrict to legal areas.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Beltsville Plant Materials Center release notes

entries.notes: Annual striate lespedeza; self-seeding warm-season legume for fescue pastures. Adds late-summer protein. Non-toxic to ruminants.
entries.source: University of Tennessee Extension forage legume guide

entries.notes: New Mexico sainfoin release; non-bloating legume for irrigated pasture. Strong second-cut performance vs other sainfoin lines.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: USDA Bozeman release; cold-hardy sainfoin. Honey-producing crop. Pair with grass for sustained hay quality.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Re-flowering sainfoin; two cuts per season possible. Lower tannins than wild types. Good honey crop.
entries.source: Montana State University Extension sainfoin guide

entries.notes: Cornell 1947 release; prostrate-growing birdsfoot trefoil. Bloat-safe pasture legume. Strong on heavy, wet, acid soils.
USDA Beltsville release; intermediate-growth birdsfoot trefoil. Reliable in mixed grass stands. Bloat-safe.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Beltsville Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Cornell winter-hardy birdsfoot release. Erect-growing for hay production. Long-time Northeast standard.
USDA Mandan release; high persistence on the northern Plains. Reseeds. Pair with smooth brome for hay.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Bismarck Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: AAFC release; Maritimes-adapted birdsfoot trefoil. Hardy to zone 3. Good fit for short cool growing seasons.
Greater birdsfoot trefoil; tolerates wet acid soils where common birdsfoot fails. Higher tannin than L. corniculatus.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Corvallis Plant Materials Center fact sheet

entries.notes: Penn State release; long-time roadside erosion species. CAUTION: invasive across the Midwest; restrict to managed embankments only.
entries.source: Penn State Extension release notes; Midwest Invasive Plant Network

entries.notes: Nebraska release; cold-hardy hairy vetch for upper Midwest. Plant with rye for grazing or cover. Hard seed reduces; less reseeding.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Manhattan Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: Auburn University southern-adapted hairy vetch. High biomass under southeastern winters. Roller-crimp at full bloom for no-till mulch.
entries.source: Auburn University Extension hairy vetch guide

entries.notes: Early-flowering Auburn vetch; matures in time for corn planting in zone 7+. Reduced winter biomass for southern systems.
Auburn University southern hairy vetch release; mid-season flowering. High biomass for cotton and corn cover cropping.
entries.source: Auburn University Extension hairy vetch guide

entries.notes: USDA southern common vetch release. White-seeded for easier visual ID in mixed cover crop stands. Lower bloat risk than other vetches.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Americus Plant Materials Center release

entries.notes: California Mediterranean vetch for winter cover and grazing. Showy purple flowers. Less cold tolerant than hairy vetch.
entries.source: University of California Cooperative Extension cover crop guide

entries.notes: Tropical legume for summer cover and grazing. Australian Tan selection; large tan seeds, high seedling vigor. Frost-killed but heavy fall biomass.
entries.source: Texas A&M AgriLife tropical legume guide

entries.notes: Early-flowering lablab; produces seed in shorter season than Tan. Useful for late-summer plantings in southern Plains.
Heirloom forage cowpea mix; iron-tan seeded. Smother weeds, fix nitrogen, fall-graze. Southern summer cover staple.
entries.source: USDA NRCS southern cowpea guide; Mississippi State Extension

entries.notes: Jefferson-era heirloom forage cowpea; speckled brown seed. Vigorous viny growth. Excellent late-summer hog and deer browse.
entries.source: Seed Savers Exchange yearbook; USDA NRCS

entries.notes: Bushy crowder type; dual-purpose food and forage cowpea. Mississippi State release. Earlier than viny types.
Cool-season climbing pea for winter cover and silage. Pair with cereal rye or triticale for trellising. Frost-tolerant.
entries.source: USDA NRCS cover crop guide; Penn State Extension

entries.notes: Spring-sown semi-leafless forage pea; semi-leafless gene tangles vines for upright stand. High silage protein.
Swedish dual-purpose green manure and forage pea. Viny habit; pair with oat or barley for haylage support.
entries.source: Saskatchewan Forage Variety Guide; Nordic plant variety register

entries.notes: Tall forage soybean; high biomass for hay and silage. Late maturity (group 7) for southern adaptation.
entries.source: University of Tennessee Extension forage soybean guide

entries.notes: Late-maturing tall-growing forage soybean. Single-cut hay or silage. Plant in 30 in rows for tall canopy.
entries.source: University of Tennessee forage soybean variety trials

entries.notes: Group 7 forage soybean; reliable Mid-South performance. Cut at R3-R5 for haylage. Strong nitrogen return.
entries.source: University of Tennessee forage soybean variety trials

entries.notes: Historic vining black-seeded forage soybean; long-standing in the South. Indeterminate vine. Cut for hay or graze.
entries.source: Mississippi State Extension forage soybean guide

entries.notes: Short-season pigeon pea selection; multi-purpose food, forage, browse. Tropical perennial north of zone 10; annual elsewhere.
entries.source: ECHO Community tropical agriculture pigeon pea guide

entries.notes: Pasja-type fast establishing forage turnip; small bulb, leafy tops. Multi-graze for sheep and dairy. Strong fall biomass.
entries.source: PGG Wrightson Seeds cultivar register; Oregon State Forage Information System

entries.notes: Tankard purple-top turnip for stockpiled winter grazing. Large bulb, sweet flesh. Strip-graze through frosts.
entries.source: DLF Pickseed cultivar register; Penn State Extension

entries.notes: Hybrid leafy turnip; little to no bulb. Fast regrowth for multi-cut grazing. High dry matter top yield.
entries.source: PGG Wrightson Seeds; Penn State Extension

entries.notes: Classic open-pollinated purple-top globe turnip for stockpile grazing. Big bulbs hold through hard frost.
Tankard-type forage turnip; high bulb-to-top ratio. Late-season feed once tops killed by frost.
Holland-bred turnip-x-Chinese-cabbage cross; quick leafy biomass. Multi-cut. Strong fit for fall finishing pastures.
Multi-graze forage rape; rapid regrowth after grazing. New Zealand release. Good for lamb finishing pastures.
Historic English forage rape; reliable winter grazing standby. Tolerates light frost. Strip-graze to limit waste.
entries.source: USDA NRCS cover crop guide; Penn State Extension

entries.notes: Multi-graze forage rape selection. High dry matter yield for ewe and lamb finishing. NZ release.
Kale-rape hybrid; very late-season palatability. Stem-heavy biomass. NZ release; common in dairy winter forage rotations.
entries.source: PGG Wrightson Seeds Winfred release notes

entries.notes: Tall English forage kale; stockpile to graze winter. Stem feed plus leaves. 3-5 ft tall in good conditions.
entries.source: UK National Institute of Agricultural Botany forage kale guide

entries.notes: Shorter forage kale, faster maturity than Maris Kestrel. Useful for mid-fall lamb finishing.
Scottish marrow-stem forage kale; thick stems for stockpile grazing. Tolerates poor weather. Strip-graze with electric fence.
Improved tall forage kale; high leaf-to-stem ratio. NZ release for dairy winter forage. Tolerates frost.
Very tall (5+ ft) forage kale; large marrow stems. Strip-graze sequentially through winter. Watch for waste.
entries.source: PGG Wrightson Seeds Goliath release notes

entries.notes: High-bulb-yielding forage swede; long-keeping in field. Suited to dairy and sheep stockpile grazing in cool climates.
Historic German forage swede; long-stand bulbs. Strong powdery mildew tolerance.
Purple-top swede selection; reliable in Scottish-style stockpile grazing. Good keeping quality through winter.
entries.source: UK NIAB forage swede variety register

entries.notes: Long-time UK forage swede release. Reliable big bulbs for winter sheep and cattle finishing. Tolerates clubroot.
entries.source: UK NIAB forage swede variety register

entries.notes: Indian fodder mulberry release for silkworm and ruminant browse. High leaf protein. Coppice annually for compact browse hedge.
entries.source: Central Sericulture Research and Training Institute (India) descriptor

entries.notes: Japanese fodder mulberry; broad-leaf high-protein browse for goats and dairy. Coppice 3-4 times per growing season.
Indian fodder mulberry release; high biomass, leaf protein 22 percent. Train as alley crop for cattle and goats.
entries.source: Central Sericulture Research and Training Institute (India) descriptor

entries.notes: Chinese tortured willow; pollarded as drought-feed for cattle and sheep. Bridge fodder species through New Zealand droughts.
Weeping willow pollard fodder, common in NZ silvopasture. Cut whole branches and drop in pasture during drought. Tannins reduce internal parasites.
Western native saline-soil browse shrub. Year-round forage for sheep and cattle. Drought tolerant; deer browse.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center fact sheet

entries.notes: Great Basin native cold desert shrub; winter sheep forage. Salt-tolerant. Slow growing; long-stand species for arid rangeland.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Great Basin plant fact sheet

entries.notes: California native large saltbush; cattle and wildlife browse. Tolerates extreme salinity. Useful for reclaiming saline pasture corners.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Lockeford Plant Materials Center fact sheet

entries.notes: Australian fodder acacia; coppice annually for sheep browse in Mediterranean climates. Salt and drought tolerant. Note: invasive in S Africa.
Tannin-rich Australian acacia; cattle and goat browse, also leather tannin source. Invasive in many subtropical regions; check before planting.
entries.source: Australia CSIRO fodder tree guide; ISSG global invasive species database

entries.notes: Athel tamarix; non-invasive sterile species used as shade and camel/sheep browse in arid SW deserts. Salt tolerant. Avoid invasive Tamarix ramosissima.
entries.source: USDA NRCS Arid Lands Plant Materials Center notes

entries.notes: Brown-midrib forage sorghum for silage; reduced lignin. Single-cut crop for chopping. Aim for boot-stage harvest.
entries.source: USDA ARS Sorghum BMR research notes

entries.notes: BMR forage sorghum with later maturity than BMR-100. Higher dry matter yield in long-season regions.
entries.source: USDA ARS Sorghum BMR research notes

entries.notes: Sweet BMR silage sorghum; high palatability and digestibility. Sugar-stem chops well for haylage and bunker silage.
Russian black-oil sunflower for silage; high oil content. Single-cut. Pair with corn or sorghum for mixed silage in dryland systems.
entries.source: Saskatchewan Forage Variety Guide; USDA GRIN sunflower descriptors

entries.notes: Tall (10+ ft) heritage Russian sunflower for silage and seed. High biomass. Cut at petal drop for silage chopping.
entries.source: Seed Savers Exchange yearbook; UNL Extension silage sunflower guide

entries.notes: Winter triticale silage variety; high biomass cut at boot stage. Pair with hairy vetch for haylage protein boost.
entries.source: Penn State Extension triticale variety guide

entries.notes: California-bred awnless triticale for silage; soft-stem palatability. Strong fall growth. Multi-cut potential.
entries.source: Resource Seeds Inc Trical variety register; UC Davis silage guide

entries.notes: Spring oat with field pea (typically Maxum or Arvika) at 100 lb oat + 60 lb pea per acre. Cut at oat soft dough for high protein silage.
entries.source: Penn State Extension small grain silage guide

entries.notes: Winter triticale plus Austrian winter pea; spring forage harvest. Cut at triticale boot for highest protein. Roll-crimp for organic systems.
entries.source: Penn State Extension small grain silage guide

entries.notes: Winter wheat with hairy vetch; soft red winter wheat with cold-tolerant vetch (Madison or Auburn) for grass-legume silage at boot stage.
entries.source: Penn State Extension small grain silage guide

entries.notes: Sudangrass x sorghum hybrid (sudex); finer stem than forage sorghum, better regrowth than sudangrass. Single-cut silage or multi-cut grazing.
entries.source: UNL Extension summer annual forage guide
